notes.content:
Balbharti [Maharashtra State Board Class 10 Maths Solutions](https://maharashtraboardsolutions.com/maharashtra-state-board-class-10-maths-solutions/) covers the Practice Set 3.1 Geometry 10th Class Maths Part 2 Answers Solutions Chapter 3 Circle.

### Class 10 Maths Part 2 Practice Set 3.1 Chapter 3 Circle Questions With Answers Maharashtra Board

Question 1.

 In the adjoining figure, the radius of a circle with centre C is 6 cm, line AB is a tangent at A. Answer the following questions.

 i. What is the measure of ∠CAB? Why?

 ii. What is the distance of point C from line AB? Why?

 iii. d(A, B) = 6 cm, find d(B, C).

 iv. What is the measure of ∠ABC? Why?

![Image 3: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.1 1](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.1-1.png?resize=245%2C119&ssl=1)

 Solution:

 i. line AB is the tangent to the circle with centre C and radius AC. [Given]

 ∴ ∠CAB = 90° (i) [Tangent theorem]

 ii. seg CA ⊥ line AB [From (i)]

 radius = l(AC) = 6 cm

 ∴ The distance of point C from line AB is 6 cm.

 iii. In ∆CAB, ∠CAB = 90° [From (i)]

 ∴ BC 2 = AB 2 + AC 2 . [Pythagoras theorem]

![Image 4: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.1 2](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.1-2.png?resize=230%2C126&ssl=1)

 = 6 2 + 6 2

 = 2 × 6 2

 ∴ BC = 2×6 2−−−−−√ [Taking square root of both sides]

 = 6 2–√ cm

 ∴ d(B, C) = 6 cm

 iv. In ∆ABC,

 AC = AB = 6cm

 ∴ ∠ABC = ∠ACB [Isosceles triangle theorem]

 Let ∠ABC = ∠ACB =x

 In ∆ABC,

 ∠CAB + ∠ABC + ∠ACB = 180° [Sum of the measures of angles of a triangle is 180°]

 ∴ 90° + x + x = 180°

 ∴ 90 + 2x = 180°

 ∴ 2x = 180°- 90°

 ∴ x = 90∘2

 ∴ x = 45°

 ∴ ∠ABC = 45°

Question 2.

 In the adjoining figure, O is the centre of the circle. From point R, seg RM and seg RN are tangent segments touching the circle at M and N. If (OR) = 10 cm and radius of the circle = 5 cm, then

 i. What is the length of each tangent segment?

 ii. What is the measure of ∠MRO?

 iii. What is the measure of ∠MRN?

![Image 5: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.1 3](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.1-3.png?resize=206%2C134&ssl=1)

 Solution:

 seg RM and seg RN are tangents to the circle with centre O. [Given]

 ∴ ∠OMR = ∠ONR = 90° [Tangent theorem]

![Image 6: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.1 4](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.1-4.png?resize=206%2C138&ssl=1)

 i. In ∆OMR, ∠OMR = 90°

 ∴ OR 2 = OM 2 + RM 2 [Pythagoras theorem]

 ∴ 10 2 = 5 2 + RM 2

 ∴ 100 = 25 + RM 2

 ∴ RM 2 = 75

 ∴ RM = 75−−√ [Taking square root of both sides]

 ∴ RM = RN [Tangent segment theorem]

 Length of each tangent segment is 5 3–√ cm.

 ii. In ∆RMO,

 ∠OMR = 90° [Tangent theorem]

 OM = 5 cm and OR = 10 cm

 ∴ OM = 1 2 OR

 ∴ ∠MRO = 30° (i) [Converse of 30° – 60° – 90° theorem]

 Similarly, ∠NRO = 30°

 iii. But, ∠MRN = ∠MRO + ∠NRO [Angle addition property]

 = 30° + 30° [From (i)]

 ∴ ∠MRN = 60°

Question 3.

 Seg RM and seg RN are tangent segments of a circle with centre O. Prove that seg OR bisects ∠MRN as well as ∠MON.

![Image 7: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.1 5](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.1-5.png?resize=205%2C134&ssl=1)

 Solution:

 Proof:

 In ∆OMR and ∆ONR,

 seg RM ≅ seg RN [Tangent segment theorem]

 seg OM ≅ seg ON [Radii of the same circle]

 seg OR ≅ seg OR [Common side]

 ∴ ∆OMR ≅ ∆ONR [SSS test of congruency]

 {∴ ∠MRO ≅ ∠NRO

 ∠MOR ≅ ∠NOR } [c.a.c.t.]

 ∴ seg OR bisects ∠MRN and ∠MON.

Question 4.

 What is the distance between two parallel tangents of a circle having radius 4.5 cm? Justify your answer.

 Solution:

 Let the lines PQ and RS be the two parallel tangents to circle at M and N respectively. Through centre O, draw line AB || line RS.

![Image 8: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.1 6](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.1-6.png?resize=193%2C148&ssl=1)

 OM = ON = 4.5 [Given]

 line AB || line RS [Construction]

 line PQ || line RS [Given]

 ∴ line AB || line PQ || line RS

 Now, ∠OMP = ∠ONR = 90° (i) [Tangent theorem]

 For line PQ || line AB,

 ∠OMP = ∠AON = 90° (ii) [Corresponding angles and from (i)]

 For line RS || line AB,

 ∠ONR = ∠AOM = 90° (iii) [Corresponding angles and from (i)]

 ∠AON + ∠AOM = 90° + 90° [From (ii) and (iii)]

 ∴ ∠AON + ∠AOM = 180°

 ∴ ∠AON and ∠AOM form a linear pair.

 ∴ ray OM and ray ON are opposite rays.

 ∴ Points M, O, N are collinear. (iv)

 ∴ MN = OM + ON [M – O – N, From (iv)]

 ∴ MN = 4.5 + 4.5

 ∴ MN = 9 cm

 ∴ Distance between two parallel tangents PQ and RS is 9 cm.

Question 1.

 In the adjoining figure, seg QR is a chord of the circle with centre O. P is the midpoint of the chord QR. If QR = 24, OP = 10, find radius of the circle. To find solution of the problem, write the theorems that are useful. Using them, solve the problem. (Textbook pg. no. 48)

![Image 9: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.1 7](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.1-7.png?resize=131%2C131&ssl=1)

 Solution:

 Theorems which are useful to find solution:

 i. The segment joining the centre of a circle and the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to the chord.

 ii. In a right angled triangle, sum of the squares of the perpendicular sides is equal to square of its hypotenuse.

 QP = 1 2 (QR) [P is the midpoint of chord QR]

![Image 10: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.1 8](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.1-8.png?resize=140%2C158&ssl=1)

1 2 × 24 = 12 units

 Also, seg OP ⊥ chord QR [The segment joining centre of a circle and midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to the chord]

 In ∆OPQ, ∠OPQ = 90°

 ∴ OQ 2 = OP 2 + QP 2 [Pythagoras theorem]

 = 10 2 + 12 2

 = 100 + 144

 = 244

 ∴ OQ = 244−−−√ = 2 61−−√ units.

 ∴ The radius of the circle is 2 61−−√ units.

Question 2.

 In the adjoining figure, M is the centre of the circle and seg AB is a diameter, seg MS ⊥ chord AD, seg MT ⊥ chord AC, ∠DAB ≅ ∠CAB.

 i. Prove that: chord AD ≅ chord AC.

 ii. To solve this problem which theorems will you use?

 a. The chords which are equidistant from the centre are equal in length.

 b. Congruent chords of a circle are equidistant from the centre.

![Image 11: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.1 9](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.1-9.png?resize=180%2C154&ssl=1)

 iii. Which of the following tests of congruence of triangles will be useful?

 a. SAS b. ASA c. SSS d. AAS e. Hypotenuse-side test.

 Using appropriate test and theorem write the proof of the above example. (Textbook pg. no, 48)

 Solution:

 Proof:

 i. ∠DAB ≅ ∠CAB [Given]

 ∴ ∠SAM ≅ ∠TAM (i) [A – S – D, A – M – B, A -T – C]

 In ∆SAM and ∆TAM,

 ∠SAM ≅ ∠TAM [From (i)]

 ∠ASM ≅ ∠ATM [Each angle is of measure 90°]

 seg AM ≅ seg AM [Common side]

 ∴ ∆SAM ≅ ∆TAM [AAS [SAA] test of congruency]

 ∴ side MS ≅ side MT [c.s.c.t]

 But, seg MS ⊥ chord AD [Given]

 seg MT ⊥chord AC

 ∴ chord AD ≅ chord AC [Chords of a circle equidistant from the centre are congruent]

 ii. Theorem used for solving the problem:

 The chords which are equidistant from the centre are equal in length.

 iii. Test of congruency useful in solving the above problem is AAS ISAAI test of congruency.

Question 3.

 i. Draw segment AB. Draw perpendicular bisector l of the segment AB. Take point P on the line l as centre,

 PA as radius and draw a circle. Observe that the circle passes through point B also. Find the reason.

 ii. Taking any other point Q on the line l, if a circle is drawn with centre Q and radius QA, will it pass through B? Think.

 iii. How many such circles can be drawn, passing through A and B? Where will their centres lie? (Textbook pg. no. 49)

 Solution:

![Image 12: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.1 10](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.1-10.png?resize=370%2C498&ssl=1)

 i. Draw the circle with centre P and radius PA.

 line l is the perpendicular bisector of seg AB.

 Every point on the perpendicular bisector of a segment is equidistant from the endpoints of the segment.

 ∴ PA = PB … [Perpendicular bisector theorem]

 ∴ PA = PB = radius

 ∴ The circle with centre P and radius PA passes through point B.

ii. The circle with any other point Q and radius QA is drawn.

 QA = QB = radius … [Perpendicular bisector theorem]

 ∴ The circle with centre Q and radius QA passes through point B.

iii. We can draw infinite number of circles passing through A and B.

 All their centres will lie on the perpendicular bisector of AB (i.e., line l)

Question 4.

 i. Take any three non-collinear points. What should be done to draw a circle passing through all these points? Draw a circle through these points.

 ii. Is it possible to draw one more circle passing through these three points? Think of it. (Textbook pg. no. 49)

 Solution:

![Image 13: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.1 11](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.1-11.png?resize=414%2C367&ssl=1)

 i. Let points A, B, C be any three non collinear points.

 Draw the perpendicular bisector of seg AB (line l).

 ∴ Points A and B are equidistant from any point of line l ….(i)[Perpendicular bisector theorem]

 Draw the perpendicular bisector of seg BC (line m) to intersect line l at point P.

 ∴ Points B and C are equidistant from any point of line m ….(ii) [Perpendicular bisector theorem]

 ∴ PA = PB …[From (i)]

 PB = PC … [From (ii)]

 ∴ PA = PB = PC = radius

 ∴ With PA as radius the required circle is drawn through points A, B, C.

 ii. It is not possible to draw more than one circle passing through these three points.

Question 5.

 Take 3 collinear points D, E, F. Try to draw a circle passing through these points. If you are not able to draw a circle, think of the reason. (Textbook pg. no. 49)

 Solution:

![Image 14: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.1 12](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.1-12.png?resize=312%2C295&ssl=1)

 Let D, E, F be the collinear points.

 The perpendicular bisector of DE and EF drawn (i.e., line l and line m) do not intersect at a common point.

 ∴ There is no single common point (centre of circle) from which a circle can be drawn passing through points D, E and F.

 Hence, we cannot draw a circle passing through points D, E and F.

Question 6.

 Which theorem do we use in proving that hypotenuse is the longest side of a right angled triangle? (Textbook pg. no. 52)

![Image 15: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.1 13](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.1-13.png?resize=171%2C87&ssl=1)

 Solution:

 In ∆ABC,

 ∠ABC = 90°

 ∴ ∠BAC < 90° and ∠ACB < 90° [Given]

 ∴ ∠ABC > ∠BAC and ∠ABC > ∠ACB

 ∴ AC > BC and AC > AB [Side opposite to greater angle is greater]

 ∴ Hypotenuse is the longest side in right angled triangle.

 We use theorem, If two angles of a triangle are not equal, then the side opposite to the greater angle is greater than the side opposite to the smaller angle.

Question 7.

 Theorem: Tangent segments drawn from an external point to a circle are congruent

 Draw radius AP and radius AQ and complete the following proof of the theorem.

 Given: A is the centre of the circle.

 Tangents through external point D touch the circle at the points P and Q.

 To prove: seg DP ≅ seg DQ

 Construction: Draw seg AP and seg AQ.

![Image 16: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.1 14](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.1-14.png?resize=227%2C138&ssl=1)

 Solution:

 Proof:

 In ∆PAD and ∆QAD,

 seg PA ≅ [segQA] [Radii of the same circle]

 seg AD ≅ seg AD [Common side]

![Image 17: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.1 15](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.1-15.png?resize=224%2C146&ssl=1)

 ∠APD = ∠AQD = 90° [Tangent theorem]

 ∴ ∆PAD = ∆QAD [By Hypotenuse side test]

 ∴ seg DP = seg DQ [c.s.c.t]

Question
- In the figure, circle centre C has radius AC = 6 cm. Line AB is tangent to the circle at A.
- (i) Find measure of ∠CAB and explain.
- (ii) Find the distance of point C from line AB and explain.
- (iii) Given d(A,B) = 6 cm (so AB = 6 cm), find d(B,C).
- (iv) Find measure of ∠ABC and explain.

Method
- A radius drawn to the point of tangency is perpendicular to the tangent line.
- The distance from a point to a line is the length of the perpendicular from the point to the line.
- For a right triangle, use the Pythagorean theorem.
- If two sides of a triangle are equal, the base angles opposite them are equal; use angle-sum of a triangle (180°).

Working
(i) Because AC is a radius and AB is tangent at A, the radius AC meets the tangent at the point of contact A at right angle. Hence ∠CAB = 90°.

(ii) The shortest distance from C to line AB is along the perpendicular from C to AB. That perpendicular is CA and its length equals the radius: CA = 6 cm. Therefore the distance from C to line AB is 6 cm.

(iii) In triangle ABC, angle at A is 90°, and AB = 6 cm (given) and AC = 6 cm (radius). By the Pythagorean theorem,
BC^2 = AB^2 + AC^2 = 6^2 + 6^2 = 36 + 36 = 72.
So BC = √72 = 6√2 cm.

(iv) Since AB = AC = 6 cm, triangle ABC is isosceles with AB = AC, so ∠ABC = ∠ACB. Let each equal x. Using angle sum,
∠CAB + ∠ABC + ∠ACB = 180°
90° + x + x = 180°
2x = 90° ⇒ x = 45°.
Thus ∠ABC = 45°.

Final answer
(i) ∠CAB = 90°.

(ii) Distance of C from line AB = 6 cm.

(iii) d(B,C) = BC = 6√2 cm.

(iv) ∠ABC = 45°.

Question  
In the figure, O is the centre of a circle. From an external point R, RM and RN are tangent segments touching the circle at M and N. Given OR = 10 cm and radius OM = ON = 5 cm, find:  
i. the length of each tangent segment;  
ii. the measure of ∠MRO;  
iii. the measure of ∠MRN.

Method  
- Use the fact that a radius to a point of tangency is perpendicular to the tangent line, so OM ⟂ RM and ON ⟂ RN.  
- Use the right triangle OMR to compute RM by Pythagoras.  
- Use the right triangle ratios to find angle ∠MRO.  
- Use symmetry (tangents from the same external point are equal and give equal angles) to find ∠MRN.

Working
1. Length of tangent RM (and RN):
   - In right triangle OMR, OM = 5 cm, OR = 10 cm, and OM ⟂ RM.
   - By Pythagoras: OR^2 = OM^2 + RM^2.
   - So RM^2 = OR^2 − OM^2 = 10^2 − 5^2 = 100 − 25 = 75.
   - RM = √75 = 5√3 cm.
   - Tangents from the same external point are equal, so RN = RM = 5√3 cm.

2. Measure of ∠MRO:
   - In right triangle OMR, the side opposite angle ∠MRO is OM (length 5) and the hypotenuse is OR (length 10).
   - sin(∠MRO) = opposite/hypotenuse = OM/OR = 5/10 = 1/2.
   - Therefore ∠MRO = 30°.
   - By the same reasoning ∠NRO = 30°.

3. Measure of ∠MRN:
   - Angle at R between RM and RN equals ∠MRO + ∠NRO = 30° + 30° = 60°.

Final answer
i. Each tangent segment RM and RN = 5√3 cm.  
ii. ∠MRO = 30°.  
iii. ∠MRN = 60°.

Question 3

Seg RM and seg RN are tangent segments of a circle with centre O. Prove that seg OR bisects ∠MRN as well as ∠MON.

Method

Show that triangles OMR and ONR are congruent and then use corresponding angles of congruent triangles to conclude that OR divides both ∠MRN and ∠MON into two equal parts.

Working

1. Since RM and RN are tangents from the same external point R to the circle, the two tangent segments are equal in length:
   RM = RN.  (Property of tangents from a common external point)

2. OM and ON are radii of the same circle, so
   OM = ON.

3. OR is a common side of triangles OMR and ONR, so
   OR = OR.

4. From (1), (2) and (3) the three sides of triangle OMR are respectively equal to the three sides of triangle ONR. Hence
   ΔOMR ≅ ΔONR by SSS congruence.

5. Corresponding angles in congruent triangles are equal. Therefore
   ∠MRO = ∠NRO.
   These are the two angles at R formed by RM and RN with OR, so OR divides ∠MRN into two equal angles. Thus OR bisects ∠MRN.

6. Also, from congruence,
   ∠MOR = ∠NOR.
   These are the two angles at O formed by OM and ON with OR, so OR divides ∠MON into two equal angles. Thus OR bisects ∠MON.

Final answer

OR bisects both ∠MRN and ∠MON.

Question
What is the distance between two parallel tangents of a circle having radius 4.5 cm? Justify your answer.

Method
- Let the two parallel tangents touch the circle at points M and N.
- Draw the centre O of the circle and consider the unique line through O perpendicular to the tangents.
- Use the fact that a radius to a point of contact is perpendicular to the tangent at that point to show M, O, N are collinear.
- Compute MN in terms of the radius.

Diagram cue: the textbook shows a circle with two parallel tangents. Do not assume any extra lengths from the figure; we only use the tangency and parallelism information given.

Working
1. Let the two parallel tangents be PQ and RS, touching the circle at M and N respectively. Let O be the centre of the circle.
2. A radius drawn to the point of contact with a tangent is perpendicular to the tangent. Hence OM ⟂ PQ and ON ⟂ RS.
3. Because PQ ∥ RS, the perpendicular to PQ through O is the same as the perpendicular to RS through O. Thus the lines OM and ON lie on the same straight line through O (they are collinear). Therefore M, O and N are collinear.
4. Since M, O, N are collinear with O between M and N, the distance MN equals OM + ON. Each of OM and ON equals the radius r = 4.5 cm.
5. So MN = r + r = 2r = 2 × 4.5 = 9 cm.

Final answer
The distance between the two parallel tangents is 9 cm.

Question

In the adjoining figure, QR is a chord of a circle with centre O. P is the midpoint of the chord QR. If QR = 24 and OP = 10, find the radius of the circle. State the theorems you use and solve the problem.

Method

Useful theorems:
1. The line joining the centre of a circle and the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to the chord.
2. In a right-angled triangle, (hypotenuse)^2 = (sum of squares of the other two sides). (Pythagoras' theorem)

Using these, notice that P is the midpoint of QR, so PQ = QR/2. Also OP is perpendicular to QR, so triangle OPQ is right-angled at P. Then use Pythagoras to find OQ (the radius).

Working

1. PQ = QR/2 = 24/2 = 12.

2. In right triangle OPQ (right angle at P),
   OQ^2 = OP^2 + PQ^2
   = 10^2 + 12^2
   = 100 + 144
   = 244.

3. Therefore OQ = sqrt(244) = sqrt(4·61) = 2·sqrt(61).

Final answer

Radius of the circle = 2√61 units.

### Diagram reference

![Worked diagram 1](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.1-7.png?resize=131%2C131&ssl=1)

solutionPages.page-6:
Question
- In the given figure M is the centre of the circle and AB is a diameter. MS ⟂ chord AD and MT ⟂ chord AC. Also ∠DAB = ∠CAB.
i. Prove that chord AD = chord AC.
ii. Which theorem is used in this problem?
iii. Which congruence test is useful here?

Method
- Show triangles ΔASM and ΔATM are congruent by using the given equal angles, the right angles from the perpendiculars, and the common side AM.
- From congruence deduce MS = MT. Then use the theorem that equal distances from the centre to chords imply the chords are equal.

Working
1. Observations and notation
   - Since AB is a diameter and M is the centre, points A, M, B are collinear. Thus the line AM is the same straight line as AB.
   - S lies on chord AD and MS ⟂ AD, so AS is along AD. T lies on chord AC and MT ⟂ AC, so AT is along AC.

2. Equal angles at A
   - Given ∠DAB = ∠CAB.
   - Replace AB by AM (because A, M, B are collinear) and replace AD by AS, AC by AT (since S on AD and T on AC). So
     ∠SAM = ∠TAM.    (corresponding angles at A)

3. Right angles at S and T
   - MS ⟂ AD ⇒ ∠ASM = 90°.
   - MT ⟂ AC ⇒ ∠ATM = 90°.
   - Therefore ∠ASM = ∠ATM.

4. Common side
   - AM is common to ΔASM and ΔATM.

5. Congruence of triangles
   - In triangles ΔASM and ΔATM we have
     ∠SAM = ∠TAM (step 2),
     ∠ASM = ∠ATM (step 3),
     AM = AM (common).
   - Thus the two triangles are congruent by the AAS congruence criterion.

6. Corresponding sides
   - From congruence, MS = MT (corresponding sides of congruent triangles).

7. Conclude about chords
   - MS and MT are the perpendicular distances from the centre M to chords AD and AC respectively.
   - Since the distances from the centre to these chords are equal (MS = MT), the chords AD and AC are equal in length (chords equidistant from the centre are equal).

Final answer
i. chord AD = chord AC. (Proof completed as above.)

ii. Theorem used: "Chords equidistant from the centre of a circle are equal in length."

iii. Useful congruence test: AAS (two angles and a corresponding side).

### Diagram reference

![Worked diagram 1](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.1-9.png?resize=180%2C154&ssl=1)
solutionPages.page-7:
Question
i. Draw segment AB. Draw its perpendicular bisector l. Take a point P on l as centre and draw a circle with radius PA. Explain why this circle also passes through B.  
ii. If Q is any other point on l and a circle is drawn with centre Q and radius QA, will it pass through B? Explain.  
iii. How many circles can be drawn that pass through both A and B? Where will their centres lie?

Method
- Use the defining property of a perpendicular bisector: it meets the segment AB at its midpoint and is perpendicular to AB.  
- Compare the distances from any point on this bisector to A and to B by looking at the two right triangles formed.  
- Conclude about membership of B on the circle and about all possible centres.

Working
1. Let M be the midpoint of AB where the perpendicular bisector l meets AB. Since l is the perpendicular bisector, AM = MB and l ⟂ AB at M.

2. Consider point P on l. Join PA and PB and also join P to M. In triangles PAM and PBM:
   - PM is common.
   - AM = MB (M is midpoint).
   - Angles PMA and PMB are right angles (PM ⟂ AB).
   Thus the two right triangles PAM and PBM are congruent (right-triangle congruence by hypotenuse–leg). Therefore PA = PB.

3. Since PA = PB and the circle drawn has centre P and radius PA, point B lies at distance PB = PA from P. Hence B lies on that circle. This proves (i).

4. The same argument applies to any other point Q on l. Let Q be on the perpendicular bisector and let the midpoint be M. Triangles QAM and QBM are congruent by the same reasoning, giving QA = QB. So a circle with centre Q and radius QA also passes through B. This proves (ii).

5. Because every point on the perpendicular bisector gives equal distances to A and B, every such point can serve as the centre of a circle through A and B. There are infinitely many points on the line l, so infinitely many such circles. All their centres lie on the perpendicular bisector l. This answers (iii).

Final answer
i. The perpendicular bisector property gives PA = PB, so the circle with centre P and radius PA passes through B.  
ii. Yes. For any Q on l, QA = QB, so the circle with centre Q and radius QA also passes through B.  
iii. Infinitely many circles can be drawn through A and B; their centres are all the points on the perpendicular bisector of AB (the line l).

### Diagram reference

![Worked diagram 1](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.1-10.png?resize=370%2C498&ssl=1)
solutionPages.page-8:
Question
i. Take any three non-collinear points. What should be done to draw a circle passing through all these points? Draw a circle through these points.  
ii. Is it possible to draw one more circle passing through these three points? Think of it.

Method
- To find the center of the circle that passes through three non-collinear points A, B, C, construct the perpendicular bisectors of two sides of triangle ABC.  
- Their intersection is the center (circumcenter) of the required circle.  
- Use a compass with this center and radius equal to the distance from the center to any one of the three points to draw the circle.  
- To check uniqueness, reason that any center of a circle through A, B, C must lie on the perpendicular bisectors of AB and BC; hence the center is unique.

Diagram cue
The textbook diagram shows triangle ABC and the intersection of the perpendicular bisectors. No numerical lengths from the diagram are needed; the construction uses only midpoints and perpendiculars.

Working
1. Let A, B, C be three non-collinear points (vertices of triangle ABC).  
2. Construct the perpendicular bisector of segment AB:
   - Find the midpoint M of AB (use compass arcs from A and B) and draw the line through M perpendicular to AB. Every point on this line is equidistant from A and B.
3. Construct the perpendicular bisector of segment BC:
   - Find the midpoint N of BC and draw the line through N perpendicular to BC. Every point on this line is equidistant from B and C.
4. Let O be the intersection point of these two perpendicular bisectors. Since O is on the bisector of AB, OA = OB. Since O is on the bisector of BC, OB = OC. Therefore OA = OB = OC.
5. With center O and radius OA (or OB or OC) draw a circle using the compass. This circle passes through A, B and C because each is at distance OA from O.
6. Uniqueness: Suppose there were another circle through A, B, C with center O'. Then O' must satisfy O'A = O'B = O'C. Hence O' lies on the perpendicular bisectors of AB and BC as well. Two distinct lines (the two perpendicular bisectors) intersect at exactly one point, so O' must coincide with O. Therefore there cannot be a different center; the circle is unique.

Final answer
i. Construction: Draw perpendicular bisectors of any two sides (for example AB and BC) of triangle ABC. Their intersection O is equidistant from A, B and C. With center O and radius OA draw the circle passing through A, B, C.

ii. No — exactly one circle (the circumcircle) passes through three non-collinear points. The center is the unique intersection of the perpendicular bisectors of the sides.

### Diagram reference

![Worked diagram 1](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.1-11.png?resize=414%2C367&ssl=1)

Question
Take three collinear points D, E, F. Try to draw a circle passing through these points. If you are not able to draw a circle, state the reason.

Method
To draw a circle through three given points we need a point (the centre) equidistant from all three points. A standard construction finds the centre as the intersection of the perpendicular bisectors of two segments joining the points (for example, of DE and EF). If those two perpendicular bisectors do not meet, no single centre exists and no such circle can be drawn.

Working
1. Let D, E, F be three distinct points lying on the same straight line ℓ.
2. Draw segment DE and construct its perpendicular bisector: this bisector is a line perpendicular to ℓ and passes through the midpoint of DE.
3. Draw segment EF and construct its perpendicular bisector: this bisector is also a line perpendicular to ℓ and passes through the midpoint of EF.
4. Both perpendicular bisectors are perpendicular to the same line ℓ, so they are parallel to each other. Parallel lines do not meet, so there is no common intersection point.
5. Any centre of a circle passing through D, E and F would have to lie on both perpendicular bisectors. Since the two bisectors do not intersect, no single point is equidistant from D, E and F.
6. Therefore there is no circle that passes through three distinct collinear points.

Diagram cue
If a textbook diagram shows the two perpendicular bisectors, you can observe they are parallel (both perpendicular to the common line through D, E, F); this is the reason they never meet to give a centre.

Final answer
No. If D, E and F are three distinct collinear points, we cannot draw a circle through all three because the perpendicular bisectors of DE and EF are parallel and do not meet; hence there is no unique centre equidistant from all three points. (If two or three of the given points coincide, that is a special degenerate case.)

### Diagram reference

![Worked diagram 1](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.1-12.png?resize=312%2C295&ssl=1)

Question
Which theorem do we use in proving that the hypotenuse is the longest side of a right‑angled triangle?

Method
Use the theorem that compares sides opposite unequal angles: in any triangle, the larger angle lies opposite the longer side. Apply this to a right triangle where the right angle is clearly larger than the other two angles.

Working
Let triangle ABC be right‑angled at B. Then
- ∠B = 90°.
- ∠A and ∠C are acute, so each is less than 90°.

Therefore ∠B > ∠A and ∠B > ∠C. By the theorem "the side opposite the greater angle is greater than the side opposite the smaller angle," the side opposite ∠B (which is AC) is longer than the sides opposite ∠A and ∠C (which are BC and AB respectively). Hence AC > AB and AC > BC.

Final answer
We use the theorem: "If two angles of a triangle are unequal, then the side opposite the greater angle is longer than the side opposite the smaller angle." This shows the hypotenuse (side opposite the right angle) is the longest side.

### Diagram reference

Question 7

Given:
- A is the centre of the circle.
- From an external point D two tangents touch the circle at P and Q.

To prove:
- DP ≅ DQ

Construction:
- Join AP and AQ.

Diagram cue:
- The diagram shows AP and AQ as radii, and DP and DQ as tangents from the external point D to the circle.

Proof/Steps:
1. AP = AQ because both are radii of the same circle.
2. At a point of contact the radius is perpendicular to the tangent. Therefore ∠APD = 90° and ∠AQD = 90°.
3. In triangles PAD and QAD:
   - Each triangle is a right triangle (right angles at P and Q respectively).
   - The hypotenuse AD is common to both triangles.
   - One corresponding leg AP equals AQ (from step 1).
4. Thus the two right triangles PAD and QAD are congruent by the right-triangle hypotenuse-leg (RHS) criterion.
5. From the congruence, corresponding sides DP and DQ are equal.

Result:
seg DP ≅ seg DQ.

notes.content:
Balbharti [Maharashtra State Board Class 10 Maths Solutions](https://maharashtraboardsolutions.com/maharashtra-state-board-class-10-maths-solutions/) covers the Practice Set 3.2 Geometry 10th Class Maths Part 2 Answers Solutions Chapter 3 Circle.

### Class 10 Maths Part 2 Practice Set 3.2 Chapter 3 Circle Questions With Answers Maharashtra Board

Question 1.

 Two circles having radii 3.5 cm and 4.8 cm touch each other internally. Find the distance between their centres.

 Solution:

 Let the two circles having centres P and Q touch each other internally at point R.

 Here, QR = 3.5 cm, PR = 4.8 cm

![Image 3: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.2 1](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.2-1.png?resize=180%2C158&ssl=1)

 The two circles touch each other internally.

 ∴ By theorem of touching circles,

 P – Q – R

 PQ = PR – QR

 = 4.8 – 3.5

 = 1.3 cm

 [The distance between the centres of circles touching internally is equal to the difference in their radii]

Question 2.

 Two circles of radii 5.5 cm and 4.2 cm touch each other externally. Find the distance between their centres.

 Solution:

 Let the two circles having centres P and R touch each other externally at point Q.

 Here, PQ = 5.5 cm, QR = 4.2 cm

![Image 4: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.2 2](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.2-2.png?resize=206%2C106&ssl=1)

 The two circles touch each other externally.

 ∴ By theorem of touching circles,

 P – Q – R

 PR = PQ + QR

 = 5.5 + 4.2

 = 9.7 cm

 [The distance between the centres of the circles touching externally is equal to the sum of their radii]

Question 3.

 If radii of two circles are 4 cm and 2.8 cm. Draw figure of these circles touching each other

 i. externally

 ii. internally.

 Solution:

 i. Circles touching externally:

![Image 5: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.2 3](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.2-3.png?resize=659%2C391&ssl=1)

 ii. Circles touching internally:

![Image 6: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.2 4](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.2-4.png?resize=420%2C387&ssl=1)

Question 4.

 In the adjoining figure, the circles with centres P and Q touch each other at R A line passing through R meets the circles at A and B respectively. Prove that –

![Image 7: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.2 5](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.2-5.png?resize=234%2C161&ssl=1)

 i. seg AP || seg BQ,

 ii. ∆APR ~ ∆RQB, and

 iii. Find ∠RQB if ∠PAR = 35°.

 Solution:

 The circles with centres P and Q touch each other at R.

 ∴ By theorem of touching circles,

 P – R – Q

 i. In ∆PAR,

 seg PA = seg PR [Radii of the same circle]

 ∴ ∠PRA ≅ ∠PAR (i) [Isosceles triangle theorem]

 Similarly, in ∆QBR,

 seg QR = seg QB [Radii of the same circle]

 ∴ ∠RBQ ≅ ∠QRB (ii) [Isosceles triangle theorem]

 But, ∠PRA ≅ ∠QRB (iii) [Vertically opposite angles]

 ∴ ∠PAR ≅ ∠RBQ (iv) [From (i) and (ii)]

 But, they are a pair of alternate angles formed by transversal AB on seg AP and seg BQ.

 ∴ seg AP || seg BQ [Alternate angles test]

 ii. In ∆APR and ∆RQB,

 ∠PAR ≅ ∠QRB [From (i) and (iii)]

 ∠APR ≅ ∠RQB [Alternate angles]

 ∴ ∆APR – ∆RQB [AA test of similarity]

 iii. ∠PAR = 35° [Given]

 ∴ ∠RBQ = ∠PAR= 35° [From (iv)]

 In ∆RQB,

 ∠RQB + ∠RBQ + ∠QRB = 180° [Sum of the measures of angles of a triangle is 180°]

 ∴ ∠RQB + ∠RBQ + ∠RBQ = 180° [From (ii)]

 ∴ ∠RQB + 2 ∠RBQ = 180°

 ∴ ∠RQB + 2 × 35° = 180°

 ∴ ∠RQB + 70° = 180°

 ∴ ∠RQB = 110°

Question 5.

 In the adjoining figure, the circles with centres A and B touch each other at E. Line l is a common tangent which touches the circles at C and D respectively. Find the length of seg CD if the radii of the circles are 4 cm, 6 cm.

![Image 8: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.2 6](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.2-6.png?resize=272%2C165&ssl=1)

 Construction : Draw seg AF ⊥ seg BD.

 Solution:

 i. The circles with centres A and B touch each other at E. [Given]

 ∴ By theorem of touching circles,

 A – E – B

![Image 9: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.2 7](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.2-7.png?resize=261%2C167&ssl=1)

 ∴ ∠ACD = ∠BDC = 90° [Tangent theorem]

 ∠AFD = 90° [Construction]

 ∴ ∠CAF = 90° [Remaining angle of ꠸AFDC]

 ∴ ꠸AFDC is a rectangle. [Each angle is of measure 900]

 ∴ AC = DF = 4 cm [Opposite sides of a rectangle]

 Now, BD = BF + DF [B – F – C]

 ∴ 6 = BF + 4 BF = 2 cm

 Also, AB = AE + EB

 = 4 + 6 = 10 cm

 [The distance between the centres of circles touching externally is equal to the sum of their radii]

ii. Now, in ∆AFB, ∠AFB = 90° [Construction]

 ∴ AB 2 = AF 2 + BF 2 [Pythagoras theorem]

 ∴ 10 2 = AF 2 + 2 2

 ∴ 100 = AF 2 + 4

 ∴ AF 2 = 96

 ∴ AF = \sqrt { 96 } [Taking square root of both sides]

 = \sqrt{16 \times 6}

 = 4 \sqrt { 6 } cm

 But, CD = AF [Opposite sides of a rectangle]

 ∴ CD = 4 \sqrt { 6 } cm

Question 1.

 Take three collinear points X – Y – Z as shown in figure.

 Draw a circle with centre X and radius XY. Draw another circle with centre Z and radius YZ.

 Note that both the circles intersect each other at the single point Y. Draw a line / through point Y and perpendicular to seg XZ. What is line l (Textbook pg. no. 56)

 Solution:

![Image 10: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.2 8](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.2-8.png?resize=385%2C280&ssl=1)

 Line l is a common tangent of the two circles.

Question 2.

 Take points Y – X – Z as shown in the figure. Draw a circle with centre Z and radius ZY.

 Also draw a circle with centre X and radius XY. Note that both the circles intersect each other at the point Y.

 Draw a line l perpendicular to seg YZ through point Y. What is line l? (Textbook pg. no. 56)

 Solution:

![Image 11: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.2 9](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.2-9.png?resize=360%2C293&ssl=1)

 Line l is a common tangent of the two circles.

If two circles in the same plane intersect with a line in the plane in only one point, they are said to be touching circles and the line is their common tangent.

The point common to the circles and the line is called their common point of contact.

1. Circles touching externally:

 For circles touching externally, the distance between their centres is equal to sum of their radii, i.e. AB = AC + BC

![Image 12: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.2 10](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.2-10.png?resize=159%2C141&ssl=1)

2. Circles touching internally:

 For circles touching internally, the distance between their centres is equal to difference of their radii,

 i. e. AB = AC – BC

![Image 13: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.2](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.2-11.jpg?resize=139%2C155&ssl=1)

Question 3.

 The circles shown in the given figure are called externally touching circles. Why? (iexthook pg. no. 57)

![Image 14: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.2 11](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.2-11.png?resize=156%2C140&ssl=1)

 Answer:

 Circles with centres R and S lie in the same plane and intersect with a line l in the plane in one and only one point T [R – T – S].

 Hence the given circles are externally touching circles.

Question 4.

 The circles shown in the given figure are called internally touching circles, why? (Textbook pg. no. 57)

![Image 15: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.2 12](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.2-12.png?resize=131%2C139&ssl=1)

 Answer:

 Circles with centres N and M lie in the same plane and intersect with a line p in the plane in one and only one point T [K – N – M].

 Hence, the given circles are internally touching circles.

Question 5.

 In the given figure, the radii of the circles with centres A and B are 3 cm and 4 cm respectively. Find

 i. d(A,B) in figure (a)

 ii. d(A,B) in figure (b) (Textbook pg. no. 57)

![Image 16: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.2 13](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.2-13.png?resize=334%2C189&ssl=1)

 Solution:

 i. Here, circle with centres A and B touch each other externally at point C.

 ∴ d(A, B) = d(A, C) + d(B ,C)

 = 3 + 4

 ∴ d(A,B) = 7 cm

 [The distance between the centres of circles touching externally is equal to the sum of their radii]

 ii. Here, circle with centres A and 13 touch each other internally at point C.

 ∴ d(A, B) = d(A, C) – d(B, C)

 = 4 – 3

 ∴ d(A,B) = 1 cm

 [The distance between the centres of circles touching internally is equal to the difference in their radii]

Question
Two circles with radii 3.5 cm and 4.8 cm touch each other internally. Find the distance between their centres.

Method
When two circles touch internally, the point of contact, and the two centres are collinear. The distance between the centres equals the difference of the radii (larger radius minus smaller radius).

Working
Let the centres be P and Q, and let the point of internal contact be R. Take PR = 4.8 cm (larger radius) and QR = 3.5 cm (smaller radius). Because P, Q, R are collinear with Q between P and R, the distance PQ is
PQ = PR − QR = 4.8 − 3.5 = 1.3 cm.

Final answer
The distance between the centres is 1.3 cm.

### Diagram reference

![Worked diagram 1](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.2-1.png?resize=180%2C158&ssl=1)

Question 2

Two circles of radii 5.5 cm and 4.2 cm touch each other externally. Find the distance between their centres.

Method

When two circles are externally tangent, the centres and the point of contact lie on a straight line. The distance between the centres equals the sum of the radii.

Working

Let the centres be P and R, and let Q be their point of contact. Then P, Q, R are collinear and
distance PR = radius of first circle + radius of second circle
= 5.5 cm + 4.2 cm
= 9.7 cm

(Diagram cue: a diagram showing two circles touching at Q with centres P and R would illustrate P–Q–R on one straight line; no additional numeric information from the diagram is needed.)

Final answer

The distance between the centres is 9.7 cm.

### Diagram reference

Question
If radii of two circles are 4 cm and 2.8 cm. Draw figures of these circles touching each other
i. externally
ii. internally.

Method
- Two circles touch externally when the distance between their centers equals the sum of their radii.
- Two circles touch internally when the distance between their centers equals the difference of their radii.
- Use a ruler (or scale) to mark the required center separation on a straight line; then draw the circles with a compass using the given radii.

Working
1. Compute the required distances between the centers.
   - For external contact: distance = sum of radii = 4 + 2.8 = 6.8 cm.
   - For internal contact: distance = difference of radii = |4 − 2.8| = 1.2 cm.

Construction steps (use a ruler, compass and pencil)

A. Circles touching externally
1. Draw a straight line l on the paper. Mark a point O1 on l — this will be the center of the circle of radius 4 cm.
2. With the ruler measure along l from O1 and mark point O2 so that O1O2 = 6.8 cm.
   - (You may measure 6.8 cm directly with the ruler, or set the compass to 6.8 cm and step it from O1 to locate O2.)
3. With compass centered at O1, draw a circle of radius 4 cm.
4. With compass centered at O2, draw a circle of radius 2.8 cm.
5. The two circles meet at exactly one point on the line O1O2; this point is their point of external tangency. Verify distances: from O1 to that point = 4 cm and from O2 to that point = 2.8 cm.

B. Circles touching internally
1. On a fresh line (or the same line l), mark a point O1 as center of the larger circle (radius 4 cm).
2. Along the line from O1 mark point O2 so that O1O2 = 1.2 cm (the difference of radii).
3. With compass centered at O1 draw the circle of radius 4 cm.
4. With compass centered at O2 draw the circle of radius 2.8 cm.
5. The smaller circle lies inside the larger one and they meet at exactly one point on the line O1O2 (at distance 4 cm from O1). Check: distance from O2 to that point = 2.8 cm, so the circles are internally tangent.

Diagram cue
The textbook shows diagrams. They only indicate positions of centers and tangency along the line joining centers. The construction steps above follow from those facts; no additional numerical information from the diagrams was assumed.

Final answer
- For external tangency: place the centers 6.8 cm apart (4 + 2.8). Draw circles of radii 4 cm and 2.8 cm at those centers; they touch externally at one point on the line joining the centers.
- For internal tangency: place the centers 1.2 cm apart (4 − 2.8). Draw the larger circle of radius 4 cm about the first center and the smaller circle of radius 2.8 cm about the second center; the smaller circle lies inside the larger and they touch internally at a single point on the line joining the centers.

### Diagram reference

Question

In the adjoining figure, two circles with centres P and Q touch each other at R. A line through R meets the circle with centre P again at A and the circle with centre Q again at B. Prove:

i. AP ∥ BQ,
ii. ΔAPR ∼ ΔRQB,
iii. If ∠PAR = 35°, find ∠RQB.

Method

- Use equal radii to identify isosceles triangles and equal base angles.
- Use the fact that when two circles touch externally at R, the centers P, R, Q are collinear.
- Compare angles formed by the same straight lines or by a transversal to conclude parallelism and similarity.
- For the numerical value, use angle relations inside triangle RQB.

Working

1. Observations from the figure (Diagram cue)
- The circles touch externally at R, so the line of centres passes through the point of contact. Hence P, R, Q are collinear.

2. Equal radii → isosceles triangles
- In triangle PAR, PA and PR are radii of the same circle, so PA = PR. Therefore triangle PAR is isosceles with PA = PR, so its base angles are equal:
  ∠PRA = ∠PAR.   (1)
- In triangle QBR, QB and QR are radii of the same circle, so QB = QR. Hence triangle QBR is isosceles and its base angles are equal:
  ∠QRB = ∠RBQ.   (2)

3. Angles formed by the same pair of lines
- The angle ∠PRA is formed by the lines PR and RA.
- The angle ∠QRB is formed by the lines QR and RB.
- Since PR and QR are the same straight line (P–R–Q) and RA and RB lie on the same straight line AB, the angle between PR and RA equals the angle between QR and RB. Thus
  ∠PRA = ∠QRB.   (3)

4. Proof of (i): AP ∥ BQ
- From (1) and (3): ∠PAR = ∠RBQ.
- ∠PAR is the angle made by AP with AB at A; ∠RBQ is the angle made by BQ with BA at B. These are alternate interior angles on the transversal AB for the pair of lines AP and BQ. Equal alternate interior angles imply the lines are parallel. Therefore
  AP ∥ BQ.   (Answer to part i)

5. Proof of (ii): ΔAPR ∼ ΔRQB
- We already have ∠PAR = ∠RBQ (from step 4).
- Because AP ∥ BQ, corresponding angles formed with the line PR (or with AB) give another equality: ∠APR = ∠RQB.
- Thus two angles of ΔAPR are equal respectively to two angles of ΔRQB, so by the AA criterion the triangles are similar:
  ΔAPR ∼ ΔRQB.   (Answer to part ii)

6. Finding ∠RQB when ∠PAR = 35°
- Given ∠PAR = 35°. From step 4, ∠RBQ = ∠PAR = 35°.
- In triangle RQB, QB = QR so base angles at R and B are equal (from (2)):
  ∠QRB = ∠RBQ = 35°.
- Sum of angles in triangle RQB:
  ∠RQB + ∠RBQ + ∠QRB = 180°
  ∠RQB + 35° + 35° = 180°
  ∠RQB + 70° = 180°
  ∠RQB = 110°.   (Answer to part iii)

Final answer

i. AP ∥ BQ.

ii. ΔAPR ∼ ΔRQB by AA similarity.

iii. ∠RQB = 110°.

### Diagram reference

Question  
In the figure, two circles with centres A and B touch each other at E. A common tangent line l touches the circles at C and D respectively. The radii are AC = 4 cm and BD = 6 cm. Find the length of CD.

Method  
Use the fact that radii to points of contact are perpendicular to the tangent. Thus AC ⟂ l and BD ⟂ l, so C and D are the feet of perpendiculars from A and B to the same line l. Draw the segment AB and form a right triangle whose legs are CD and the difference of the radii; apply the Pythagorean theorem.

Working
1. Because the circles touch externally, AB = AC + BD = 4 + 6 = 10 cm.

2. Since AC ⟂ l and BD ⟂ l, the segment joining the centres A and B is perpendicular to neither but the perpendicular distances from A and B to l are 4 cm and 6 cm respectively. The vertical separation of the centres (perpendicular to l) is |6 − 4| = 2 cm.

3. Let CD = x. The triangle with vertices A, B and one of the contact points projects to a right triangle whose legs are x (horizontal separation between the feet C and D) and 2 (vertical separation of centres). The hypotenuse is AB = 10. By Pythagoras,
   x^2 + 2^2 = 10^2
   x^2 + 4 = 100
   x^2 = 96
   x = √96 = √(16·6) = 4√6.

Final answer  
CD = 4√6 cm (approximately 9.80 cm).

Question
- Three collinear points X — Y — Z are given. A circle with centre X and radius XY and another circle with centre Z and radius YZ meet at the single point Y. A line l through Y is drawn perpendicular to segment XZ. What is the line l?

Method
- Use the standard property: for any circle, the radius drawn to a point of contact is perpendicular to the tangent at that point.
- Apply this to both circles at the common point Y.

Working
1. XY is a radius of the circle with centre X, and ZY is a radius of the circle with centre Z.
2. Since X, Y, Z are collinear, both radii XY and ZY lie along the line XZ.
3. Line l is given as perpendicular to XZ, so l is perpendicular to XY and also perpendicular to ZY at point Y.
4. For each circle, the line through Y perpendicular to its radius at Y is a tangent to that circle at Y. Therefore l is tangent to the circle with centre X and also tangent to the circle with centre Z.
5. Because l is tangent to both circles at the same point Y, l is a common tangent at the point where the two circles touch.

Final answer
- Line l is the common tangent to the two circles at the point Y (the common point of contact).

### Diagram reference

![Worked diagram 1](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.2-8.png?resize=385%2C280&ssl=1)

Question
Take points Y – X – Z as shown (so Y, X, Z are collinear with X between Y and Z). Draw a circle with centre Z and radius ZY, and a circle with centre X and radius XY. Both circles pass through Y. Draw the line l through Y perpendicular to YZ. What is line l?

Method
Show that the radii to Y are collinear, so the line through Y perpendicular to YZ is perpendicular to both radii; a line perpendicular to a radius at the point of contact is a tangent. Conclude whether l is a tangent to one or both circles and describe the contact.

Working
1. From the given notation Y – X – Z, the points Y, X, Z lie on one straight line with X between Y and Z. Hence the segments XY and YZ lie on the same straight line.

2. The radii to the common point Y are:
   - For the circle with centre X: radius XY.
   - For the circle with centre Z: radius ZY.
   Both these radii lie along the same straight line YXZ.

3. Line l is drawn through Y and is perpendicular to YZ. Since YZ is the same line as YX, line l is perpendicular to both XY and ZY (the two radii) at Y.

4. A line perpendicular to the radius at the point where it meets the circle is a tangent to that circle at that point. Therefore l is tangent to the circle with centre X at Y and also tangent to the circle with centre Z at Y.

5. Check tangency type: distance between centres X and Z equals XZ. Because X lies between Y and Z,
   ZY = ZX + XY  ⇒ ZX = ZY − XY.
   Thus XZ = ZY − XY = (larger radius) − (smaller radius).
   That shows the distance between centres equals the difference of the radii, so the two circles touch each other internally at Y.

Final answer
Line l is the common tangent to both circles at Y. The two circles touch each other internally at Y, and Y is their common point of contact.

Question 3

Given  
Two circles lie in the same plane with centres R and S. They meet the same line l in exactly one common point T, and the points are collinear in the order R — T — S.

To prove  
The two circles are externally touching (i.e., they touch each other at T from outside).

Proof / Steps
1. Let the radius of the circle with centre R be r1 and the radius of the circle with centre S be r2.  
2. Because T is a point on the first circle, RT = r1. Because T is a point on the second circle, ST = r2.  
3. Since R, T, S are collinear with T between R and S, the distance RS equals the sum of the two segments RT and TS. That is, RS = RT + TS.  
4. Substitute the radii: RS = r1 + r2.  
5. When the distance between the centres of two circles equals the sum of their radii, the circles meet at exactly one point and are tangent to each other externally at that point. Here that point is T.

Result  
Because RS = r1 + r2 and the circles have exactly one common point T with R—T—S collinear, the circles are externally touching at T.

### Diagram reference

![Worked diagram 1](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.2-11.png?resize=156%2C140&ssl=1)

Question 4

Given
- Two circles in the same plane have centres N and M and meet at a single common point T (the figure shows one circle inside the other touching at T).

To prove
- The two circles are internally touching (i.e. they have exactly one common point and one circle lies inside the other).

Proof / Steps
1. Let r_N be the radius of the circle with centre N and r_M the radius of the circle with centre M. Without loss of generality assume r_N > r_M (so the circle with centre M is the smaller one).

2. Because T is a common point of the two circles, NT = r_N and MT = r_M.

3. At a point where a circle touches another circle (a point of tangency), the tangent line there is perpendicular to the radius drawn to the point of contact. The same tangent at T is therefore perpendicular to both NT and MT. Two lines through T that are both perpendicular to the same tangent must lie on the same straight line; hence N, T and M are collinear and T lies on the line segment NM.

4. Since N, T, M are collinear with T between N and M, the distance between the centres equals the difference of the radii:
   NM = |NT − MT| = |r_N − r_M|.

5. Because the centres are closer than the sum of radii and exactly at the difference of radii, the circles meet in exactly one point and the smaller circle lies inside the larger one. This is the definition of internal tangency (internally touching).

Result
- The circles touch internally: they have exactly one common point T, the centres N, T, M are collinear, and the distance between the centres equals the difference of their radii, so one circle lies inside the other and they are internally tangent at T.

Diagram cue
- The figure shows the two circles meeting at point T with the smaller circle inside the larger; the reasoning above uses only the fact of a single common point and the centres N and M.

### Diagram reference

Question
In the given figures the radii of the circles with centres A and B are 3 cm and 4 cm respectively. Find
i. d(A, B) in figure (a)
ii. d(A, B) in figure (b)

Diagram cue
The textbook figures show:
- (a) the two circles touching each other externally at a common point C,
- (b) one circle touching the other internally at a common point C.
We use these touchings and the given radii to compute the centre-to-centre distances.

Method
When two circles touch at a point C, the centres A, C and B are collinear.
- If the circles touch externally, C lies between A and B, so AB = AC + BC.
- If the circles touch internally, one centre lies between the other centre and the point of tangency, so AB = |BC − AC|.

Working
Given: AC = radius of circle centered at A = 3 cm, BC = radius of circle centered at B = 4 cm.

i. Figure (a): external contact at C
Since A, C, B are collinear with C between A and B,
AB = AC + BC = 3 cm + 4 cm = 7 cm.

ii. Figure (b): internal contact at C
Since A, C, B are collinear with one centre inside the other,
AB = |BC − AC| = |4 cm − 3 cm| = 1 cm.

Final answer
i. d(A, B) = 7 cm
ii. d(A, B) = 1 cm

notes.content:
Balbharti [Maharashtra State Board Class 10 Maths Solutions](https://maharashtraboardsolutions.com/maharashtra-state-board-class-10-maths-solutions/) covers the Practice Set 3.3 Geometry 10th Class Maths Part 2 Answers Solutions Chapter 3 Circle.

### Class 10 Maths Part 2 Practice Set 3.3 Chapter 3 Circle Questions With Answers Maharashtra Board

Question 1.

 In the adjoining figure, points G, D, E, F are concyclic points of a circle with centre C.

 ∠ECF = 70°, m(arc DGF) = 200°. Find m(arc DE) and m(arc DEF).

![Image 3: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.3 1](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.3-1.png?resize=141%2C130&ssl=1)

 Solution:

 m(arc EF) = m∠ECF [Definition of measure of minor arc]

 ∴ m(arc EF) = 70°

 i. m(arc DE) + m(arc DGF)

 + m(arc EF) = 360° [Measure of a circle is 360°]

 ∴ m(arc DE) = 360° – m(arc DGF) – m(arc EF)

 = 360° – 200° – 70°

 ∴ m(arc DE) = 90°

 ii. m(arc DEF) = m(arc DE) + m(arc EF) [Arc addition property]

 = 90° + 70°

 ∴ m(arc DEF) = 160°

Question 2.

 In the adjoining figure, AQRS is an equilateral triangle. Prove that,

 i. arc RS ≅ arc QS ≅ arc QR

 ii. m(arc QRS) = 240°.

![Image 4: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.3 2](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.3-2.png?resize=134%2C134&ssl=1)

 Solution:

 Proof:

 i. ∆QRS is an equilateral triangle, [Given]

 ∴ seg RS ≅ seg QS ≅ seg QR [Sides of an equilateral triangle]

 ∴ arc RS ≅ arc QS ≅ arc QR [Corresponding arcs of congruents chords of a circle are congruent]

 ii. Let m(arc RS) = m(arc QS)= m(arc QR) = x

 m(arc RS) + m(arc QS) + m(arc QR) = 360° [Measure of a circle is 360°, arc addition property]

 ∴ x + x + x = 360°

 ∴ 3x = 360°

 ∴ x = 360∘3=120∘

 ∴ m(arc RS) = m(arc QS) = m(arc QR) = 120° (i)

 Now, m(arc QRS) = m(arc QR) + m(arc RS) [Arc addition property]

 = 120° + 120° [From (i)]

 ∴ m(arc QRS) = 240°

Question 3.

 In the adjoining figure, chord AB ≅ chord CD. Prove that, arc AC = arc BD.

![Image 5: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.3 3](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.3-3.png?resize=160%2C114&ssl=1)

 Solution:

 Proof:

 chord AB ≅ chord CD [Given]

 ∴ arc AB ≅ arc CD [Corresponding arcs of congruents chords of a circle are congruent]

 ∴ m(arc AB) = m(arc CD)

 ∴ m(arc AC) + m(arc BC) = m(arc BC) + m(arc BD) [Arc addition property]

 ∴ m(arc AC) = m(arc BD)

 ∴ arc AC ≅ arc BD

**Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Chapter 3 Circle Intext Questions and Activities**

Question 1.

 Theorem : The chords corresponding to congruent arcs of a circle (or congruent circles) are congruent. (Textbook pg. no. 61)

 Given: B is the centre of circle.

 arc APC ≅ arc DQE

 To prove: chord AC ≅ chord DE

![Image 6: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.3 5](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.3-5.png?resize=168%2C171&ssl=1)

 Proof:

 [m(arc APC) = ∠ABC (i) [Definition of measure of

 m(arc DQE) = ∠DBE] (ii) minor arc]

 arc APC ≅ arc ∠DQE (iii) [Given]

 ∴ ∠ABC ≅ ∠DBE [From (i), (ii) and (iii)]

 In ∆ABC and ∆DBE,

 side AB ≅ side DB [Radil of the same circle]

 side [CB] side [EB] [Radii of the same circle]

 ∠ABC ≅∠DBE [From (iii), Measures of congruent arcs]

 ∴ ∆ABC ≅ ∆DBE [SAS test of congruency]

 ∴ chord AC ≅ chord DE [c.s.c.t]

Question 2.

 Theorem: Corresponding arcs of congruent chords of a circle (or congruent circles) are congruent (Textbook pg. no. 61)

 Given: O is the centre of circle, chord PQ = chord RS

 To prove: arc PMQ = arc RNS

![Image 7: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.3 4](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.3-4.png?resize=174%2C167&ssl=1)

 Proof:

 In ∆POQ and ∆ROS,

 [side PO ≅ side RO

 side OQ ≅ side OS] [Radii of the same circle]

 chord PQ ≅ chord RS [Given]

 ∴ ∆POQ ≅ ∆ROS [SSS test of congruency]

 ∴ ∠POQ ≅ ∠ROS (i) [c.a.c.t.]

 m(arc PMQ) = ∠POQ (ii)

 m(arc RNS) = ∠ROS (iii) [Definition of measure of minor arc]

 ∴ arc PMQ ≅ arc RNS [From (i), (ii) and (iii)]

Question 3.

 Prove the two theorems on textbook pg.no.61 for congruent circles. (Textbook pg. no. 62)

 Theorem : The chords corresponding to congruent arcs of congruent circles are congruent

 Given: In congruent circles with centres B and R,

 arc APC ≅ arc DQE

 To prove: chord AC ≅ chord DE

![Image 8: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.3 6](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.3-6.png?resize=263%2C138&ssl=1)

 Proof:

 [m(arc APC) = ∠ABC (i)

 m(arc DQE) = ∠DRE] (ii) [Definition of measure of minor arc]

 arc APC ≅ arc DQE (iii) [Given]

 ∴ ∠ABC = ∠DRE (iv) [From (i), (ii) and (iii)]

 In ∆ABC and ∆DRE,

 [side AB ≅ side DR [Radii of congruent circles]

 side CB ≅ side ER] [From (iv)]

 ∠ABC ≅ ∠DRE

 ∴ ∆ABC ≅ ∆DRE [SAS test of congruency]

Question 4.

 While proving the first theorem of the two, we assume that the minor arc APC and minor arc DQE are congruent. Can you prove the same theorem by assuming that corresponding major arcs congruent? (Textbook pg. no. 62)

 Statement:

 The chords corresponding to congruent major arcs of a circle are congruent.

 Given: B is the centre of circle.

 arc AXC ≅ arc DXE

 To prove: chord AC ≅ chord DE

![Image 9: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.3 7](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.3-7.png?resize=168%2C177&ssl=1)

 Proof:

 m(major arc) = 360° – m(minor arc)

 ∴ m(arc AXC) = 360° – m(arc APC) (i)

 m(arc DXE) = 360° – m(arc DQE) (ii)

 m(arc AXC) = m(arc DXE) (iii) [Given]

 ∴ 360° – m(arc APC) = 360°- m(arc DQE) [From (i), (ii) and (iii)]

 ∴ m(arc APC) = m(arc DQE) (iv)

 ∴ m(arc APC) = ∠ABC (v) [Definition of measure of minor arc]

 m(arc DQE) = ∠DBE (vi)

 ∴ ∠ABC = ∠DBE (vii) [From (iv), (v) and (vi)]

 In ∆ABC and ∆DBE,

 [side AB ≅ side DB

 Side CB ≅ side EB] [Radii of the same circle]

 ∠ABC ≅ ∠DBE [From (vii)]

 ∴ ∆ABC ≅ ∆DBE [SAS test of congruency]

 ∴ chord AC ≅ chord DE [c.s.c.t.]

Question 5.

 i. In the second theorem, are the major arcs corresponding to congruent chords congruent?

 ii. Is the theorem true, when the chord PQ and chord RS are diameters of the circle? (Textbook pg. no. 62)

 Solution:

 i. Yes, the major arcs corresponding to congruent chords are congruent.

![Image 10: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.3 8](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.3-8.png?resize=182%2C180&ssl=1)

 Proof:

Question

In the adjoining figure, points G, D, E, F are concyclic points of a circle with centre C.

∠ECF = 70°, m(arc DGF) = 200°. Find m(arc DE) and m(arc DEF).

Diagram cue: The diagram is not provided here, but the text states C is the centre and ECF is an angle at the centre, so ∠ECF is the central angle subtending arc EF. No other diagram quantities are required.

Method

- Use the fact that a central angle equals the measure of its intercepted arc: m(arc EF) = m∠ECF.
- Arcs around the circle add to 360°. The circle is partitioned by arcs DE, DGF and EF, so m(arc DE) + m(arc DGF) + m(arc EF) = 360°.
- Arc DEF is the arc from D through E to F, so m(arc DEF) = m(arc DE) + m(arc EF).

Working

1. From the central angle:
   m(arc EF) = m(∠ECF) = 70°.

2. Use the full circle:
   m(arc DE) + m(arc DGF) + m(arc EF) = 360°.
   Substitute known values:
   m(arc DE) + 200° + 70° = 360°.
   m(arc DE) = 360° − 200° − 70° = 90°.

3. Arc DEF is DE + EF:
   m(arc DEF) = m(arc DE) + m(arc EF) = 90° + 70° = 160°.

Final answer

- m(arc DE) = 90°
- m(arc DEF) = 160°

### Diagram reference

![Worked diagram 1](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.3-1.png?resize=141%2C130&ssl=1)

Question
In the adjoining figure, AQRS is an equilateral triangle. Prove that:
i. arc RS ≅ arc QS ≅ arc QR
ii. m(arc QRS) = 240°.

Diagram cue: The statement as printed is ambiguous about the role of A. The steps below use only the fact that triangle QRS is equilateral (its three vertices lie on the same circle). Any extra point A shown in the figure is not needed for this proof.

Method
- Use properties of an equilateral triangle and properties of a circle:
  1. In an equilateral triangle the three sides are equal.
  2. Equal chords of a circle subtend equal arcs.
  3. The measures of the three equal arcs around a circle add to 360°.
  4. An arc that spans two adjacent equal arcs has measure equal to their sum.

Working
1. From the given, triangle QRS is equilateral. Therefore
   QR = RS = QS. These three segments are chords of the circle passing through Q, R, S.

2. In a circle, equal chords cut off equal arcs. Hence the arcs corresponding to these chords are equal:
   arc QR ≅ arc RS ≅ arc QS.

   Let the common measure be x°:
   m(arc QR) = m(arc RS) = m(arc QS) = x°.

3. The three arcs QR, RS and QS together make the entire circumference, so their measures add to 360°:
   x + x + x = 360°
   3x = 360°
   x = 120°.

   Thus m(arc QR) = m(arc RS) = m(arc QS) = 120°.

4. The arc QRS means the arc from Q to S passing through R; that arc is the union of arcs QR and RS. Therefore
   m(arc QRS) = m(arc QR) + m(arc RS) = 120° + 120° = 240°.

Final answer
i. arc RS ≅ arc QS ≅ arc QR (each has measure 120°).
ii. m(arc QRS) = 240°.

### Diagram reference

![Worked diagram 1](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.3-2.png?resize=134%2C134&ssl=1)

Question 3

In the adjoining figure, chord AB ≅ chord CD. Prove that arc AC = arc BD.

Given
- Chord AB ≅ chord CD.
- (Diagram cue) The figure shows the four points A, B, C, D on the circle in that cyclic order, so arc AC goes from A through B to C, and arc BD goes from B through C to D.

To prove
- arc AC ≅ arc BD.

Proof / Steps
1. A basic property of circles states: equal chords subtend equal arcs. From AB ≅ CD we get arc AB ≅ arc CD.

2. Because the points lie in order A–B–C–D around the circle, the measure of arc AC is the sum of the measures of arc AB and arc BC:
   m(arc AC) = m(arc AB) + m(arc BC).

   Similarly, arc BD is the sum of arc BC and arc CD:
   m(arc BD) = m(arc BC) + m(arc CD).

3. Replace m(arc AB) by m(arc CD) (from step 1) in the expression for m(arc AC):
   m(arc AC) = m(arc CD) + m(arc BC).

   Rearranging the terms (addition is commutative) gives
   m(arc AC) = m(arc BC) + m(arc CD) = m(arc BD).

4. Since the measures of arc AC and arc BD are equal, the arcs themselves are congruent:
   arc AC ≅ arc BD.

Result
arc AC ≅ arc BD.

### Diagram reference

![Worked diagram 1](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.3-3.png?resize=160%2C114&ssl=1)

Question
Given: B is the centre of a circle. arc APC ≅ arc DQE.
To prove: chord AC ≅ chord DE.

Diagram cue: The diagram shows a circle with centre B. Points A, P, C lie on one arc (with P between A and C) and points D, Q, E lie on another arc (with Q between D and E). No numerical lengths are given.

Given
- B is the centre of the circle.
- arc APC ≅ arc DQE.

To prove
- chord AC ≅ chord DE.

Proof/Steps
1. Congruent arcs have equal measures. Since arc APC ≅ arc DQE, their measures are equal; therefore the central angles that subtend these arcs are equal. The central angle subtending arc AC is ∠ABC and the central angle subtending arc DE is ∠DBE. So
   ∠ABC = ∠DBE.

2. Radii of the same circle are equal. Thus
   AB = DB and CB = EB.

3. Consider triangles ΔABC and ΔDBE. In these triangles we have
   - AB = DB (radii),
   - CB = EB (radii),
   - ∠ABC = ∠DBE (from step 1).
   These give two sides and the included angle equal in the two triangles. Hence ΔABC ≅ ΔDBE by the SAS congruence criterion.

4. From the congruence of the triangles, the corresponding sides AC and DE are equal (corresponding parts of congruent triangles are equal).

Result
chord AC ≅ chord DE.

### Diagram reference

![Worked diagram 1](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.3-5.png?resize=168%2C171&ssl=1)

Question 2

Given:
- O is the centre of a circle.
- Chord PQ = Chord RS.

Diagram cue:
- Points M and N lie on the circle such that arc PMQ is the arc from P to Q through M, and arc RNS is the arc from R to S through N. No numerical lengths or extra labels are assumed.

To prove:
- arc PMQ ≅ arc RNS.

Proof / Steps:

1. Consider triangles ΔPOQ and ΔROS. Their sides are:
   - PO and RO — both are radii of the same circle, so PO = RO.
   - OQ and OS — both are radii of the same circle, so OQ = OS.
   - PQ and RS — equal by the given.

2. Thus all three corresponding sides of ΔPOQ and ΔROS are equal. By the SSS test of congruency, ΔPOQ ≅ ΔROS.

3. From the congruence of these triangles, their corresponding angles at the centre are equal. Hence ∠POQ = ∠ROS.

4. A central angle subtends the corresponding minor arc and the measure of a minor arc equals the measure of its central angle. Therefore
   - measure(arc PMQ) = ∠POQ,
   - measure(arc RNS) = ∠ROS.

5. Combining steps 3 and 4 gives measure(arc PMQ) = measure(arc RNS), so arc PMQ ≅ arc RNS.

Result:
arc PMQ is congruent to arc RNS.

### Diagram reference

![Worked diagram 1](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.3-4.png?resize=174%2C167&ssl=1)
solutionPages.page-6:
Question 3

Given:
- Two congruent circles with centres B and R.
- arc APC ≅ arc DQE.

To prove:
- chord AC ≅ chord DE

Proof/Steps:
1. Each central angle measures the arc it subtends. Let ∠ABC be the central angle at B subtending arc APC, and let ∠DRE be the central angle at R subtending arc DQE. Since arc APC ≅ arc DQE, their central angles are equal:
   ∠ABC = ∠DRE.   (central angle — arc measure correspondence)

2. Points A and C lie on the circle with centre B, so BA and BC are radii of that circle. Thus
   BA = BC.   (radii of the same circle)

   Similarly, points D and E lie on the circle with centre R, so RD and RE are radii of that circle. Thus
   RD = RE.   (radii of the same circle)

3. The two circles are congruent, so their radii are equal. Hence
   BA = RD and BC = RE.   (equal radii of congruent circles)

4. Consider triangles ΔABC and ΔDRE.
   - AB = RD (from step 3),
   - BC = RE (from step 3),
   - ∠ABC = ∠DRE (from step 1).

   Therefore, by the SAS congruence criterion, ΔABC ≅ ΔDRE.

5. Corresponding sides of congruent triangles are equal. Hence chord AC in the first circle equals chord DE in the second:
   AC = DE.

Result:
Chord AC is congruent to chord DE.

### Diagram reference

![Worked diagram 1](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.3-6.png?resize=263%2C138&ssl=1)
solutionPages.page-7:
Question 4

Given
- B is the centre of the circle.
- Major arc AXC ≅ major arc DXE.

To prove
- chord AC ≅ chord DE.

Proof / Steps
1. For any arc, measure(major arc) = 360° − measure(minor arc). Hence
   - measure(arc AXC) = 360° − measure(arc APC),
   - measure(arc DXE) = 360° − measure(arc DQE).

2. Since measure(arc AXC) = measure(arc DXE) (given), subtracting both sides from 360° gives
   measure(arc APC) = measure(arc DQE).
   Thus the corresponding minor arcs APC and DQE are congruent.

3. The measure of a minor arc equals the measure of the central angle that subtends it. With B as centre,
   - measure(arc APC) = ∠ABC,
   - measure(arc DQE) = ∠DBE.
   Therefore ∠ABC = ∠DBE.

4. AB = DB and CB = EB because they are radii of the same circle.

5. In triangles ABC and DBE we have AB = DB, CB = EB and ∠ABC = ∠DBE. By the SAS congruence test, ∆ABC ≅ ∆DBE.

6. Corresponding parts of congruent triangles are equal, so AC = DE. These are the chords corresponding to the given congruent major arcs.

Result
chord AC ≅ chord DE.

Diagram cue: The argument uses only that B is the centre and the given equality of the two major arcs; no additional numerical lengths from the diagram are required.

### Diagram reference

![Worked diagram 1](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.3-7.png?resize=168%2C177&ssl=1)
solutionPages.page-8:
Question 5

Method
- Use congruence of triangles formed by joining the circle centre to the chord endpoints to compare central angles.
- Equal central angles give equal measures of corresponding minor arcs.
- Major arcs are the complements (with respect to 360°) of the corresponding minor arcs; equal minors give equal majors.
- For diameters show each subtends a semicircle of 180°.

Diagram cue: A diagram would typically show a circle with centre O and chords PQ and RS. All required relations (radii to endpoints, chord equalities) are derivable from these labels; no additional numerical values are assumed.

Working

(i) Major arcs corresponding to congruent chords

1. Let O be the centre of the circle. Consider chords PQ and RS which are given equal: PQ = RS.

2. Join O to P, Q, R, S. Since OP, OQ, OR, OS are radii of the same circle, we have
   OP = OR and OQ = OS.

3. In triangles POQ and ROS:
   - OP = OR (radii),
   - OQ = OS (radii),
   - PQ = RS (given).
   By SSS, triangles POQ and ROS are congruent.

4. From congruence, corresponding central angles are equal:
   ∠POQ = ∠ROS.

5. The measure of a minor arc equals the measure of its central angle. Hence the minor arc subtended by PQ has the same measure as the minor arc subtended by RS:
   m(minor arc subtending PQ) = m(minor arc subtending RS).

6. Denote the measure of a minor arc by m_min. The corresponding major arc measure is 360° − m_min. If the two minor arcs are equal, their complements with respect to 360° are also equal. Therefore the major arcs subtended by PQ and RS are equal in measure.

Thus, yes — the major arcs corresponding to congruent chords are congruent.

(ii) The special case when PQ and RS are diameters

1. If PQ is a diameter, it divides the circle into two semicircular arcs; each semicircular arc has measure 180°. The same holds for RS when it is a diameter.

2. Therefore the arcs determined by the diameters PQ and RS each measure 180°. They are equal.

Note: For a diameter there is no distinct smaller or larger arc — both arcs are semicircles of equal measure.

Final answer
(i) Yes. If two chords are congruent, their corresponding major arcs are congruent because congruent chords give equal central angles (hence equal minor arcs) and equal minors imply equal majors (both are 360° minus the same value).

(ii) Yes. If the chords are diameters, each determines a semicircular arc of 180°, so the corresponding arcs are equal.
