notes.content:
Balbharti [Maharashtra State Board Class 10 Maths Solutions](https://maharashtraboardsolutions.com/maharashtra-state-board-class-10-maths-solutions/) covers the Practice Set 3.4 Geometry 10th Class Maths Part 2 Answers Solutions Chapter 3 Circle.

### Class 10 Maths Part 2 Practice Set 3.4 Chapter 3 Circle Questions With Answers Maharashtra Board

Question 1.

 In the adjoining figure, in a circle with centre O, length of chord AB is equal to the radius of the circle. Find measure of each of the following.

 i. ∠AOB

 ii. ∠ACB

 iii. arc AB

 iv. arc ACB.

![Image 3: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.4 1](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.4-1.png?resize=141%2C171&ssl=1)

 Solution:

 i. seg OA = seg OB = radius…… (i) [Radii of the same circle]

 seg AB = radius…… (ii) [Given]

 ∴ seg OA = seg OB = seg AB [From (i) and (ii)]

 ∴ ∆OAB is an equilateral triangle.

 ∴ m∠AOB = 60° [Angle of an equilateral triangle]

 ii. m ∠ACB = 1 2 m ∠AOB [Measure of an angle subtended by an arc at a point on the circle is half of the measure of the angle subtended by the arc at the centre]

 = 1 2 × 60°

 ∴ m ∠ACB = 30°

 iii. m(arc AB) = m ∠AOB [Definition of measure of minor arc]

 ∴ m(arc AB) = 60°

 iv. m(arc ACB) + m(arc AB) = 360° [Measure of a circle is 360°]

 ∴ m(arc ACB) = 360° – m(arc AB)

 = 360° – 60°

 ∴ m(arc ACB) = 300°

Question 2.

 In the adjoining figure, ꠸PQRS is cyclic, side PQ ≅ side RQ, ∠PSR = 110°. Find

 i. measure of ∠PQR

 ii. m (arc PQR)

 iii. m (arc QR)

 iv. measure of ∠PRQ

![Image 4: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.4 2](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.4-2.png?resize=141%2C146&ssl=1)

 Solution:

 i. ꠸PQRS is a cyclic quadrilateral. [Given]

 ∴ ∠PSR + ∠PQR = 180° [Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary]

 ∴ 110° + ∠PQR = 180°

 ∴ ∠PQR = 180° – 110°

 ∴ m ∠PQR = 70°

 ii. ∠PSR= 1 2 m (arcPQR) [Inscribed angle theorem]

 110°= 1 2 m (arcPQR)

 ∴ m(arc PQR) = 220°

 iii. In ∆PQR,

 side PQ ≅ side RQ [Given]

 ∴ ∠PRQ = ∠QPR [Isosceles triangle theorem]

 Let ∠PRQ = ∠QPR = x

 Now, ∠PQR + ∠QPR + ∠PRQ = 180° [Sum of the measures of angles of a triangle is 180°]

 ∴ ∠PQR + x + x= 180°

 ∴ 70° + 2x = 180°

 ∴ 2x = 180° – 70°

 ∴ 2x = 110°

 ∴ x=110∘2=55∘

 ∴ ∠PRQ = ∠QPR = 55°….. (i)

 But, ∠QPR = 1 2 m(arc QR) [Inscribed angle theorem]

 ∴ 55° = 1 2 m(arc QR)

 ∴ m(arc QR) = 110°

 iv. ∠PRQ = ∠QPR =55° [From (i)]

 ∴ m ∠PRQ = 55°

Question 3.

 □ MRPN is cyclic, ∠R = (5x -13)°, ∠N = (Ax + 4)°. Find measures of ∠R and ∠N.

 Solution:

 □ MRPN is a cyclic quadrilateral. [Given]

 ∴ ∠R + ∠N = 180° [Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary]

![Image 5: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.4 3](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.4-3.png?resize=133%2C138&ssl=1)

 ∴ 5x – 13 + 4x + 4 = 180

 ∴ 9x – 9 = 180

 ∴ 9x = 189

 ∴ x = 189 9

 ∴ x = 21

 ∴ ∠R = 5x – 13

 = 5 × 21 – 13

 = 105 – 13

 = 92°

 ∠N = 4x + 4

 = 4 × 21 +4

 = 84 +4

 = 88°

 ∴ m∠R = 92° and m ∠N = 88°

Question 4.

 In the adjoining figure, seg RS is a diameter of the circle with centre O. Point T lies in the exterior of the circle. Prove that ∠RTS is an acute angle.

 Given: O is the centre of the circle, seg RS is the diameter of the circle.

 To prove: ∠RTS is an acute angle.

 Construction: Let seg RT intersect the circle at point P. Join PS and PT.

![Image 6: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.4 4](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.4-4.png?resize=152%2C148&ssl=1)

 Proof:

 seg RS is the diameter. [Given]

 ∴ ∠RPS = 90° [Angle inscribed in a semicircle]

 Now, ∠RPS is the exterior angle of ∆PTS.

 ∴ ∠RPS > ∠PTS [Exterior angle is greater than the remote interior angles]

![Image 7: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.4 5](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.4-5.png?resize=152%2C158&ssl=1)

 ∴ 90° > ∠PTS

 i.e. ∠PTS < 90°

 i.e, ∠RTS < 90° [R – P -T]

 ∠RTS is an acute angle.

Question 5.

 Prove that, any rectangle is a cyclic quadrilateral.

 Given: ꠸ABCD is a rectangle.

 To prove: ꠸ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral.

![Image 8: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.4 6](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.4-6.png?resize=162%2C127&ssl=1)

 Proof:

 ꠸XBCD is a rectangle. [Given]

 ∴ ∠A = ∠B = ∠C = ∠D = 90° [Angles of a rectangle]

 Now, ∠A + ∠C = 90° + 90°

 ∴ ∠A + ∠C = 180°

 ∴ ꠸ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral. [Converse of cyclic quadrilateral theorem]

Question 6.

 In the adjoining figure, altitudes YZ and XT of ∆WXY intersect at P. Prove that,

 i. □ WZPT is cyclic.

 ii. Points X, Z, T, Y are concyclic.

 Given: seg YZ ⊥ side XW

 seg XT ⊥ side WY

 To prove: i. □WZPT is cyclic.

 ii. Points X, Z, T, Y are concyclic.

![Image 9: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.4 7](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.4-7.png?resize=220%2C162&ssl=1)

 Proof:

 i. segYZ ⊥ side XW [Given]

 ∴∠PZW = 90°…… (i)

 seg XT I side WY [Given]

 ∴ ∠PTW = 90° ……(ii)

 ∠PZW + ∠PTW = 90° + 90° [Adding (i) and (ii)]

 ∴∠PZW + ∠PTW = 180°

 ∴□WZPT Ls a cyclic quadrilateral. [Converse of cyclic quadrilateral theorem]

 ii. ∠XZY = ∠YTX = 90° [Given]

 ∴ Points X and Y on line XY subtend equal angles on the same side of line XY.

 ∴ Points X, Z, T and Y are concydic. [If two points on a given line subtend equal angles at two distinct points which lie on the same side of the line, then the four points are concyclic]

Question 7.

 In the adjoining figure, m (arc NS) = 125°, m(arc EF) = 37°, find the measure of ∠NMS.

 Solution:

![Image 10: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.4 8](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.4-8.png?resize=195%2C152&ssl=1)

 Chords EN and FS intersect externally at point M.

Question 8.

 In the adjoining figure, chords AC and DE intersect at B. If ∠ABE = 108°, m(arc AE) = 95°, find m (arc DC).

 Solution:

 Chords AC and DE intersect internally at point B.

 ∴ ∠ABE = 1 2 [m(arc AE) + m(arc DC)]

 ∴ 108° = 1 2 [95° + m(arc DC)]

 ∴ 108° × 2 = 95° + m(arc DC)

 ∴ m(arc DC) = 216° – 95°

 ∴ m(arc DC) = 121°

Question
In a circle with centre O, chord AB has length equal to the radius of the circle. Find the measures of:
i. ∠AOB
ii. ∠ACB
iii. arc AB (minor arc)
iv. arc ACB (the other arc)

Method
- Use equal radii to compare OA and OB with the given chord AB.
- If three sides of triangle OAB are equal, it is equilateral, so all its interior angles are 60°.
- Use the relation: an inscribed angle subtending an arc equals half the central angle subtending the same arc.
- The measure of a minor arc equals the measure of its central angle; the remaining (major) arc measure is 360° minus the minor arc.

Diagram cue
Point C lies on the circle (on the arc opposite O), so ∠ACB is an inscribed angle that subtends arc AB.

Working
1. Let the radius be R. Then OA = R and OB = R (radii of the circle). Given AB = R.
2. Thus OA = OB = AB = R, so triangle OAB has three equal sides and is equilateral.
3. All interior angles of an equilateral triangle are 60°, so ∠AOB = 60°.
4. Angle ∠ACB is an inscribed angle subtending arc AB. An inscribed angle equals half the central angle subtending the same arc. Therefore
   ∠ACB = (1/2) ∠AOB = (1/2) × 60° = 30°.
5. The measure of minor arc AB equals the central angle ∠AOB, so arc AB = 60°.
6. The other arc ACB is the remainder of the circle: arc ACB = 360° − arc AB = 360° − 60° = 300°.

Final answer
i. ∠AOB = 60°
ii. ∠ACB = 30°
iii. arc AB = 60°
iv. arc ACB = 300°

Question
In the adjoining figure, PQRS is a cyclic quadrilateral, PQ ≅ RQ, and ∠PSR = 110°. Find
i. measure of ∠PQR
ii. m(arc PQR)
iii. m(arc QR)
iv. measure of ∠PRQ

Diagram cue: P, Q, R, S are points on the same circle. Arc PQR means the arc from P to R that passes through Q.

Method
- Use the property that opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary.
- Use the inscribed-angle theorem: an inscribed angle equals half the measure of its intercepted arc.
- Use isosceles triangle facts: equal sides imply equal base angles, and angle sum of a triangle is 180°.

Working
1. Find ∠PQR.
- In cyclic quadrilateral PQRS, opposite angles ∠PSR and ∠PQR are supplementary.
- Given ∠PSR = 110°, so ∠PQR = 180° − 110° = 70°.

2. Find m(arc PQR).
- Angle ∠PSR is an inscribed angle that intercepts arc PQR (the arc from P to R through Q).
- Therefore 110° = (1/2)·m(arc PQR) ⇒ m(arc PQR) = 2·110° = 220°.

3. Find m(arc QR).
- In triangle PQR, PQ ≅ RQ, so the angles at P and R are equal: ∠QPR = ∠PRQ = x.
- Sum of angles: ∠PQR + ∠QPR + ∠PRQ = 180° ⇒ 70° + x + x = 180° ⇒ 2x = 110° ⇒ x = 55°.
- Angle ∠QPR is an inscribed angle intercepting arc QR, so ∠QPR = (1/2)·m(arc QR).
- Thus 55° = (1/2)·m(arc QR) ⇒ m(arc QR) = 110°.

4. Find ∠PRQ.
- From step 3, ∠PRQ = 55°.

Final answer
i. ∠PQR = 70°
ii. m(arc PQR) = 220°
iii. m(arc QR) = 110°
iv. ∠PRQ = 55°

Question 3

MRPN is a cyclic quadrilateral, ∠R = (5x − 13)°, ∠N = (Ax + 4)°. Find measures of ∠R and ∠N.

Note: The symbol "A" in (Ax + 4)° appears to be a typographical error. We proceed assuming it means 4, so ∠N = (4x + 4)°. If a different value for A was intended, the problem is ambiguous and must state that value.

Method

- In a cyclic quadrilateral, each pair of opposite angles are supplementary (their measures add to 180°).
- Use this property to form an equation in x from ∠R + ∠N = 180°, solve for x, then substitute back to find each angle measure.
- Check the results by verifying the two angles sum to 180°.

Working

1. Using the cyclic property:
   (5x − 13) + (4x + 4) = 180

2. Combine like terms:
   5x − 13 + 4x + 4 = 180
   9x − 9 = 180

3. Solve for x:
   9x = 180 + 9 = 189
   x = 189 ÷ 9 = 21

4. Find the angles:
   ∠R = 5x − 13 = 5(21) − 13 = 105 − 13 = 92°
   ∠N = 4x + 4 = 4(21) + 4 = 84 + 4 = 88°

5. Check: 92° + 88° = 180°, so the supplementary condition holds.

Final answer

∠R = 92° and ∠N = 88°.

Question 4

Given:
- O is the centre of the circle.
- RS is a diameter of the circle.
- Point T lies outside the circle.

To prove:
- ∠RTS is an acute angle.

Construction:
- Let the line RT meet the circle again at P (P ≠ R). Join P to S and P to T.

Proof / Steps:
1. Since RS is a diameter, the chord RS subtends a semicircle. Any angle formed on the circle by the endpoints R and S has measure 90°. Therefore ∠RPS = 90°.
2. Points R, P and T are collinear by construction, so PR is a straight extension of PT (or PT is the extension of PR). Thus the angle ∠RPS is an exterior angle of triangle PTS at vertex P.
3. In triangle PTS, an exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles. Hence
   ∠RPS = ∠PTS + ∠PST.
4. Substituting ∠RPS = 90° gives
   ∠PTS + ∠PST = 90°.
   Both ∠PTS and ∠PST are positive, so each is less than 90°. In particular ∠PTS < 90°.
5. Because R, P, T are collinear, the angle ∠PTS (with sides PT and PS) equals the angle ∠RTS (with sides TR and TS). Therefore ∠RTS = ∠PTS < 90°.

Result:
∠RTS is an acute angle.

Question 5

Given
- ABCD is a rectangle.

To prove
- Quadrilateral ABCD is cyclic.

Diagram cue
- The figure shows rectangle ABCD with each interior angle a right angle. The diagram may show diagonals AC and BD meeting at O; we will only use facts that follow from the rectangle definition (right angles and opposite sides parallel and equal).

Proof/Steps

Method 1 (using opposite angles)
1. In a rectangle every interior angle is a right angle. Hence
   ∠A = ∠B = ∠C = ∠D = 90°.
2. Consider a pair of opposite angles, for example ∠A and ∠C. Their sum is
   ∠A + ∠C = 90° + 90° = 180°.
3. A quadrilateral is cyclic if a pair of its opposite angles are supplementary (sum to 180°). By this converse result, ABCD is cyclic.

Method 2 (constructive — using diagonals)
1. A rectangle is a parallelogram, so its diagonals AC and BD bisect each other; let O be their point of intersection. Then O is the midpoint of AC and of BD, so OA = OC = (1/2)AC and OB = OD = (1/2)BD.
2. By the Pythagorean theorem in right triangles of the rectangle,
   AC^2 = AB^2 + BC^2 and BD^2 = BC^2 + CD^2.
   Since AB = CD and BC = AD in a rectangle, BD^2 = BC^2 + AB^2 = AC^2, so BD = AC.
3. From AC = BD it follows that (1/2)AC = (1/2)BD, hence OA = OB = OC = OD. Thus O is equidistant from all four vertices.
4. Therefore a circle centered at O with radius OA passes through A, B, C, D; so ABCD is cyclic.

Result
- In either method we conclude that rectangle ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral.

Question 6

Given
- In triangle WXY, YZ is an altitude to side XW (so YZ ⟂ XW) and XT is an altitude to side WY (so XT ⟂ WY).
- The two altitudes YZ and XT meet at P (so P lies on both YZ and XT).

To prove
i. Quadrilateral WZPT is cyclic.
ii. Points X, Z, T, Y are concyclic.

Proof

(i) Show WZPT is cyclic
1. Since YZ is an altitude and P lies on YZ, points P, Y, Z are collinear. Because YZ ⟂ XW and Z lies on XW, the line PZ is perpendicular to ZW. Hence ∠PZW = 90°.
2. Since XT is an altitude and P lies on XT, points P, X, T are collinear. Because XT ⟂ WY and T lies on WY, the line PT is perpendicular to TW. Hence ∠PTW = 90°.
3. The two opposite angles ∠PZW and ∠PTW add to 90° + 90° = 180°, so a pair of opposite angles of quadrilateral WZPT are supplementary.
4. If a quadrilateral has a pair of opposite angles supplementary, the quadrilateral is cyclic. Therefore WZPT is a cyclic quadrilateral.

(ii) Show X, Z, T, Y are concyclic
1. Point Z lies on XW and on YZ. Because YZ ⟂ XW, the angle between ZX and ZY is a right angle: ∠XZY = 90°.
2. Point T lies on WY and on XT. Because XT ⟂ WY, the angle between TX and TY is also a right angle: ∠XTY = 90°.
3. Thus ∠XZY = ∠XTY. These two equal angles are subtended by the same chord XY (each is an angle standing on XY).
4. When two points (here Z and T) on the same side of a line XY see the segment XY under equal angles, those four points X, Z, T, Y lie on a common circle. Hence X, Z, T, Y are concyclic.

Result
i. WZPT is a cyclic quadrilateral.
ii. Points X, Z, T, Y lie on one circle (are concyclic).

Question
In the figure, m(arc NS) = 125° and m(arc EF) = 37°. Chords (secants) from the external point M meet the circle at E, N and at F, S. Find the measure of ∠NMS.

Method
When two secants (or two chords produced as secants) meet at an external point, the measure of the angle formed equals one-half the difference of the measures of the intercepted arcs:
m(angle) = 1/2 [measure of far arc − measure of near arc].
Here the far intercepted arc is arc NS and the nearer intercepted arc is arc EF, so
m∠NMS = 1/2 [m(arc NS) − m(arc EF)].

Diagram cue
The result uses only that the two lines through M meet the circle in points E, N and F, S so that the outer intersections determine arcs NS and EF. No other numerical lengths or labels from the diagram are needed.

Working
m∠NMS = 1/2 [m(arc NS) − m(arc EF)]
= 1/2 [125° − 37°]
= 1/2 [88°]
= 44°.

Final answer
m∠NMS = 44°.

Question  
In the figure, chords AC and DE meet at an interior point B. Given ∠ABE = 108° and m(arc AE) = 95°, find m(arc DC).

Method  
Use the theorem: an angle formed by two chords that intersect inside a circle has measure equal to half the sum of the measures of the arcs intercepted by the angle and its vertical opposite angle. For ∠ABE the intercepted arcs are arc AE and arc DC.

Working
1. By the interior chord intersection theorem,
   ∠ABE = 1/2 [m(arc AE) + m(arc DC)].

2. Substitute the known values:
   108° = 1/2 [95° + m(arc DC)].

3. Multiply both sides by 2:
   216° = 95° + m(arc DC).

4. Solve for m(arc DC):
   m(arc DC) = 216° − 95° = 121°.

Final answer  
m(arc DC) = 121°.

Question
Draw a circle with centre C and a chord AB. Take a point D on the major arc AB and a point E on the minor arc AB. Do the following measurements and comparisons:
i. Measure ∠ADB and ∠ACB and compare them.
ii. Measure ∠ADB and ∠AEB. Add the measures.
iii. Take points F, G, H on the same arc ADB (the major arc). Measure ∠AFB, ∠AGB, ∠AHB. Compare these with each other and with ∠ADB.
iv. Take a point I on the arc AEB (the minor arc). Measure ∠AIB and compare it with ∠AEB.

Method
We use standard geometry facts about angles subtended by the same chord:
- An angle subtended at the centre (vertex at C) by a chord equals the measure of the arc cut off by that chord.
- An angle subtended at any point on the circumference by the same chord equals half the measure of that arc.
From these facts we get the relations used below. Where helpful we join the centre C to A, B and the chosen point on the circle and use the isosceles triangles formed by radii.

Working

Part (i)
- Let x = ∠ADB (angle at the circumference subtended by chord AB).
- Angle ∠ACB is the central angle subtended by the same chord AB.
- The central angle measures the whole arc AB; any angle at the circumference that subtends the same arc measures half that arc.
- Therefore ∠ACB = 2 · ∠ADB.

So the central angle is twice the corresponding inscribed (circumference) angle.

Part (ii)
- ∠ADB and ∠AEB are two inscribed angles subtending chord AB but they stand on opposite arcs: D is on the major arc, E on the minor arc.
- The two arcs that these angles intercept are complementary around the circle and their measures add to 360°.
- Each inscribed angle measures half of its intercepted arc, so the sum of the two inscribed angles is half of (measure of the major arc + measure of the minor arc) = half of 360° = 180°.
- Hence ∠ADB + ∠AEB = 180°.

Part (iii)
- Points F, G, H lie on the same arc ADB as D, so each of ∠AFB, ∠AGB, ∠AHB subtends the same arc AB as ∠ADB.
- Any two inscribed angles subtending the same arc are equal.
- Therefore ∠AFB = ∠AGB = ∠AHB = ∠ADB.

Part (iv)
- Point I lies on the same arc AEB as E, so both ∠AIB and ∠AEB subtend the same arc AB (the minor arc).
- Hence ∠AIB = ∠AEB.

Final answer
i. ∠ACB = 2 · ∠ADB.

ii. ∠ADB + ∠AEB = 180°.

iii. ∠AFB = ∠AGB = ∠AHB = ∠ADB.

iv. ∠AIB = ∠AEB.

Question

Draw a sufficiently large circle with centre C. Draw any diameter PQ. Take any points R, S, T on the circle (on either semicircle). Measure ∠PRQ, ∠PSQ, ∠PTQ. What do you observe?

Method

1. Draw circle with centre C and diameter PQ.  
2. Choose any point R on the circle and join CR, CP and CQ. (Repeat for S and T.)  
3. Use geometry (angle chasing and isosceles triangles) to find the measure of the angle subtended by chord PQ at the point on the circle.

Working

Take a point R on the circle and join CR, CP and CQ.

- CP, CQ and CR are radii, so CP = CR and CQ = CR.
- In triangle CPR, since CP = CR, the base angles at P and R are equal. Let each be x. So
  ∠CPR = ∠PRC = x.
  Then the third angle at C in triangle CPR is ∠PCR = 180° − 2x.
- In triangle CQR, since CQ = CR, the base angles at Q and R are equal. Let each be y. So
  ∠CQR = ∠QRC = y.
  Then the third angle at C in triangle CQR is ∠RCQ = 180° − 2y.

Now look at the straight line PCQ: P, C and Q are collinear because PQ is a diameter, so the angle PCQ is a straight angle of 180°. But PCQ is made up of the two adjacent angles at C found above:
∠PCQ = ∠PCR + ∠RCQ = (180° − 2x) + (180° − 2y) = 360° − 2(x + y).

Since ∠PCQ = 180°, we have
360° − 2(x + y) = 180°,
so 2(x + y) = 180°,
hence x + y = 90°.

The angle at R subtended by chord PQ is
∠PRQ = ∠PRC + ∠CRQ = x + y = 90°.

The same reasoning applies to any other point (S or T) chosen on the circle. Therefore each inscribed angle subtending the diameter PQ is a right angle.

Final answer

∠PRQ = ∠PSQ = ∠PTQ = 90°. (An angle in a semicircle is a right angle.)

Question
Prove that if two lines containing chords of a circle meet at a point outside the circle, then the measure of the angle between them equals one half the difference of the measures of the arcs intercepted by the angle.

Given
- A circle and two secant lines through an external point E.
- One secant meets the circle at A and B (A nearer E, B farther). The other secant meets the circle at C and D (C nearer E, D farther).

To prove
∠AEC = (1/2)[m(arc AC) − m(arc BD)].

Construction
Draw chord AD.

Proof / Steps
1. Note the directions of the rays:
   - The ray EA is the extension of the chord AB beyond A.
   - The ray EC is the extension of the chord CD beyond C.
   Reversing both rays (EA to AB and EC to CD) does not change the measure of the angle between them. Hence
   ∠AEC = angle between AB and DC. (We will compute this latter angle inside the circle.)

2. Express the angle between AB and DC using the chord AD:
   - ∠DAB is the inscribed angle at A formed by chords AD and AB.
   - ∠ADC is the inscribed angle at D formed by chords AD and DC.
   The angle between AB and DC equals the difference of these two inscribed angles:
   angle between AB and DC = ∠ADC − ∠DAB.
   Therefore
   ∠AEC = ∠ADC − ∠DAB.    (★)

3. Apply the Inscribed Angle Theorem:
   - ∠ADC is an inscribed angle that subtends arc AC, so
     ∠ADC = (1/2) m(arc AC).
   - ∠DAB is an inscribed angle that subtends arc DB, so
     ∠DAB = (1/2) m(arc DB).

4. Substitute these into (★):
   ∠AEC = (1/2) m(arc AC) − (1/2) m(arc DB)
         = (1/2) [m(arc AC) − m(arc BD)].

Result
∠AEC = (1/2)[m(arc AC) − m(arc BD)], as required.

Question
Given the figure of a circle with centre C, points P, Q, R, S, T on the circumference and the inscribed angles ∠PQR and ∠PSR that subtend the same arc PTR.

Given: C is the centre of the circle. ∠PQR and ∠PSR are inscribed angles intercepting arc PTR.

To prove: ∠PQR ≅ ∠PSR

Diagram cue: The diagram places points P, Q, R, S, T on the circle so that the sides of ∠PQR meet the circle at P and R, and the sides of ∠PSR also meet the circle at P and R; the arc from P to R passing through T is the intercepted arc PTR.

Method
Use the Inscribed Angle Theorem: the measure of an inscribed angle equals half the measure of its intercepted arc. Show both inscribed angles intercept the same arc; then their measures are equal.

Proof / Steps
1. Identify intercepted arcs.
   - The sides of ∠PQR meet the circle at P and R, so the intercepted arc is the arc from P to R that lies opposite Q. In the diagram this arc is the arc passing through T, denoted arc PTR. Thus arc PTR is intercepted by ∠PQR.
   - Similarly, the sides of ∠PSR meet the circle at P and R, so the intercepted arc for ∠PSR is also arc PTR.

2. Apply the Inscribed Angle Theorem.
   - By the Inscribed Angle Theorem, the measure of an inscribed angle equals half the measure of its intercepted arc. Therefore
     m∠PQR = (1/2) · m(arc PTR),
     and m∠PSR = (1/2) · m(arc PTR).

3. Compare the two measures.
   - Since both angles equal one half of the same arc measure, we have
     m∠PQR = m∠PSR.

Result
Therefore ∠PQR ≅ ∠PSR; inscribed angles that intercept the same arc are congruent.

Answers to the parts asked in the question
i. The arc intercepted by ∠PQR is arc PTR.
ii. The arc intercepted by ∠PSR is arc PTR.
iii. Relation: An inscribed angle equals half the measure of its intercepted arc; therefore any two inscribed angles intercepting the same arc are equal in measure.

Question
Angle inscribed in a semicircle is a right angle. With the help of given figure write ‘Given’, ‘To prove’ and ‘the proof’.

Given
- M is the centre of the circle.
- A, B, C are points on the circle.
- The arc AXC (the arc intercepted by ∠ABC) is a semicircle.

Diagram cue
The figure shows A and C as endpoints of the semicircle (so AC is a diameter passing through the centre M) and B is a point on the circle that subtends the semicircular arc AXC. No numerical lengths are assumed from the diagram.

To prove
∠ABC = 90°.

Proof / Steps
1. An inscribed angle equals half the measure of its intercepted arc. Therefore
   ∠ABC = 1/2 · m(arc AXC).

2. The intercepted arc AXC is a semicircle, so its measure is 180°. Thus
   m(arc AXC) = 180°.

3. Substitute this into step 1:
   ∠ABC = 1/2 · 180° = 90°.

Result
∠ABC = 90°, so an angle inscribed in a semicircle is a right angle.

Question

Theorem: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary.

Given: Quadrilateral ABCD is cyclic (all four vertices lie on a circle).

To prove: ∠B + ∠D = 180° and ∠A + ∠C = 180°.

Given
- ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral.

To prove
- ∠B + ∠D = 180°
- ∠A + ∠C = 180°

Diagram cue
- ABCD is drawn on a circle so each vertex lies on the circle. No other numerical values are assumed from the diagram.

Proof / Steps

1. Recall the Inscribed Angle Theorem: an inscribed angle equals half the measure of its intercepted arc. In notation, if an inscribed angle intercepts arc XY Z, then its measure = (1/2)·m(arc XYZ).

2. Consider ∠ADC. It is an inscribed angle that intercepts arc ABC. By the inscribed angle theorem,
   ∠ADC = (1/2)·m(arc ABC).         (i)

3. Consider ∠ABC. It is an inscribed angle that intercepts arc ADC. By the inscribed angle theorem,
   ∠ABC = (1/2)·m(arc ADC).         (ii)

4. Add (i) and (ii):
   ∠ADC + ∠ABC = (1/2)·m(arc ABC) + (1/2)·m(arc ADC)
                = (1/2)·[m(arc ABC) + m(arc ADC)].

5. The two arcs arc ABC and arc ADC together are the whole circle, so
   m(arc ABC) + m(arc ADC) = 360°.

6. Therefore
   ∠D + ∠B = (1/2)·360° = 180°,
   which shows ∠B and ∠D are supplementary.

7. A similar argument works for the other pair of opposite angles. ∠A intercepts arc BCD and ∠C intercepts arc DAB; those two arcs together make the whole circle, so
   ∠A = (1/2)·m(arc BCD),  ∠C = (1/2)·m(arc DAB),
   and ∠A + ∠C = (1/2)·[m(arc BCD) + m(arc DAB)] = (1/2)·360° = 180°.

Result

∠B + ∠D = 180° and ∠A + ∠C = 180°. Thus opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary.

Given
- ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral.
- ∠B + ∠D = 180° (already proved).

To prove
- ∠A + ∠C = 180°.

Proof/Steps
1. The sum of the interior angles of any quadrilateral is 360°. (Reason: sum of interior angles of an n‑sided polygon = (n − 2) × 180°; for n = 4 this gives 2 × 180° = 360°.)
2. Therefore,
   ∠A + ∠B + ∠C + ∠D = 360°.
3. Substitute the given relation ∠B + ∠D = 180° into the above sum:
   ∠A + (∠B + ∠D) + ∠C = 360°
   ⇒ ∠A + 180° + ∠C = 360°.
4. Subtract 180° from both sides:
   ∠A + ∠C = 360° − 180° = 180°.

Result
∠A + ∠C = 180°, as required.

Question 8

Given
- ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral.
- ∠BCE is the exterior angle at vertex C (so point E lies on the extension of CD beyond C).

To prove
- ∠BCE ≅ ∠BAD

Proof/Steps
1. Since E is on the straight line obtained by extending CD through C, the angles ∠BCE and ∠BCD form a linear pair. Therefore
   ∠BCE + ∠BCD = 180°.

2. In a cyclic quadrilateral the measures of a pair of opposite angles sum to 180°. Hence for ABCD,
   ∠BAD + ∠BCD = 180°.

3. The right-hand sides of the two equations above are equal (both 180°), so
   ∠BCE + ∠BCD = ∠BAD + ∠BCD.

4. Subtracting ∠BCD from both sides yields
   ∠BCE = ∠BAD.

Result
∠BCE is congruent to ∠BAD, as required.

Question 9

Given
- In quadrilateral ABCD, ∠A + ∠C = 180°.

To prove
- ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral (all four vertices lie on a single circle).

Proof / Steps
1. Suppose, for contradiction, that ABCD is not cyclic.  
   (Three non‑collinear points among A, B, D determine a unique circle.) Draw the circle through A, B and D.

2. The line through C and D meets this circle again at a point E (E ≠ D). Thus D, E, C are collinear and A, B, D, E lie on the same circle, so ABED is a cyclic quadrilateral.

3. From the property of a cyclic quadrilateral, opposite angles sum to 180°. Hence, in cyclic ABED,
   ∠DAB + ∠DEB = 180°.                                  (1)

   From the given for ABCD,
   ∠DAB + ∠DCB = 180°.                                  (2)

   Comparing (1) and (2) gives
   ∠DEB = ∠DCB.                                          (3)

4. Consider the triangle BEC (whose vertices are B, E and C). There are two possible arrangements of C relative to the circle; both lead to contradiction.

   Case I — C lies outside the circle (so the order on the line is D — E — C):  
   - Here ED and EC are oppositely directed rays, so the angle ∠DEB is an exterior angle of triangle BEC (it is formed by the extension ED of the side EC and the side EB).  
   - On the other hand ∠DCB is an interior angle of triangle BEC (formed by CB and CE).  
   - An exterior angle of a triangle cannot be equal to an interior angle at a different vertex of the same triangle. Thus ∠DEB ≠ ∠DCB, contradicting (3).

   Case II — C lies inside the circle (so the order on the line is D — C — E):  
   - Now ED and EC point in the same direction, so ∠DEB is an interior angle at E of triangle BEC, whereas ∠DCB is an exterior angle at C of the same triangle.  
   - Again an interior angle at one vertex cannot equal an exterior angle at a different vertex of the same triangle. So ∠DEB ≠ ∠DCB, contradicting (3).

5. In both possible positions of C relative to the circle we obtain a contradiction. Therefore the assumption that D is not on the circle through A, B and D is false.

Result
- D must lie on the circle through A, B and D; hence A, B, C, D are concyclic. Therefore ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral.

Question 10

Given:
- Points B and C lie on the same side of the line AD.
- ∠ABD = ∠ACD.

To prove:
- Points A, B, C, D are concyclic (i.e., A, B, C, D lie on one circle).

Diagram cue:
- A diagram showing points A and D on a line, and points B and C on the same side of this line, is implied. No other numerical distances or labels from the diagram are assumed.

Proof / Steps:

1. Consider the circle Γ that passes through the three non-collinear points A, B and D. Such a circle exists and is unique.

2. Let the second intersection of Γ with the line AC be E (E ≠ A). Note that E exists because the line AC meets Γ at A and at another point (unless C already lies on Γ, in which case the result is immediate).

3. Because B and E lie on the same circle Γ and both subtend the chord AD, the angles they make with the chord AD are equal:
   ∠ABD = ∠AED.    (angles in the same segment of a circle)

4. By the given hypothesis ∠ABD = ∠ACD. Combining with step 3 gives
   ∠AED = ∠ACD.    (1)

5. Now use the fact that A, E, C are collinear. Two possible orders of these three collinear points are possible; consider each and derive a contradiction unless E coincides with C.

   Case I: A — E — C (E lies between A and C).
   - Because E is between A and C, the ray CE is the same as the ray CA. Hence the angle ∠ACD (angle between CA and CD) equals ∠ECD (angle between CE and CD).
   - From (1) we have ∠AED = ∠ECD.
   - But in triangle ECD, ∠AED is an exterior angle at vertex E. By the exterior-angle property,
     ∠AED = ∠ECD + ∠EDC,
     so ∠AED > ∠ECD (since ∠EDC > 0).
   - This contradicts ∠AED = ∠ECD. Hence E cannot lie between A and C.

   Case II: A — C — E (C lies between A and E).
   - Here the ray CA is opposite to the ray CE. From (1) we have ∠AED = ∠ACD.
   - Because C is between A and E, the angle ∠CED equals the angle supplementary to ∠AED, and the angle ∠ACD becomes the exterior angle of triangle ECD.
   - The exterior-angle property for triangle ECD gives
     ∠ACD (= exterior angle) = ∠CED + ∠EDC,
     so ∠ACD > ∠CED.
   - But from (1) and the collinearity arrangement we obtain ∠CED = ∠ACD, which is impossible because it would force ∠EDC = 0.
   - Thus this order also leads to a contradiction.

6. The above two cases exhaust the possibilities for the position of E on line AC. Both lead to contradictions unless E coincides with C. Therefore the second intersection E of Γ with line AC must be C itself. Hence C lies on Γ.

7. Since Γ passes through A, B, C and D, all four points A, B, C, D are concyclic.

Result:
- A, B, C, D lie on the same circle; □ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral.

Question 11

Given
- The converse theorem states: "If four points are concyclic, then the line joining any two points subtends equal angles at the other two points which are on the same side of that line."

To prove (the original theorem)
- Given four points A, B, C, D lying on the same circle (i.e. A, B, C, D are concyclic).
- Prove that the chord AB subtends equal angles at C and at D on the same side of AB; that is, prove ∠ACB = ∠ADB.

Proof/Steps
1. Let O be the centre of the circle through A, B, C, D.
2. Consider the chord AB. The arc AB (the arc of the circle between A and B on the side containing C and D) is intercepted by both ∠ACB and ∠ADB.
3. By the inscribed-angle property: an angle subtended by an arc at a point on the circle equals half the measure of the central angle that subtends the same arc. Thus
   - ∠ACB = 1/2 × (measure of arc AB),
   - ∠ADB = 1/2 × (measure of arc AB).
4. Since both angles intercept the same arc AB, their measures are equal:
   ∠ACB = ∠ADB.

Result
- If four points A, B, C, D lie on a circle, then the angles subtended by chord AB at C and at D on the same side of AB are equal. (This is the theorem whose converse was given.)

### Class 10 Maths Part 2 Practice Set 3.5 Chapter 3 Circle Questions With Answers Maharashtra Board

Question 1.

 In the adjoining figure, ray PQ touches the circle at point Q. PQ = 12, PR = 8, find PS and RS.

 Solution:

 i. Ray PQ is a tangent to the circle at point Q and seg PS is the secant. [Given]

 ∴ PR × PS = PQ 2 [Tangent secant segments theorem]

![Image 3: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.5 1](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.5-1.png?resize=162%2C136&ssl=1)

 ∴ 8 × PS = 12 2

 ∴ 8 × PS = 144

 ∴ PS = 144 8

 ∴ PS = 18 units

 ii. Now, PS = PR + RS [P – R – S]

 ∴ 18 = 8 + RS

 ∴ RS = 18 – 8

 ∴ RS = 10 units

Question 2.

 In the adjoining figure, chord MN and chord RS intersect at point D.

 i. If RD = 15, DS = 4, MD = 8 find DN

 ii. If RS = 18, MD = 9, DN = 8 find DS

![Image 4: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.5](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.5-2-1.jpg?resize=171%2C140&ssl=1)

 Solution:

 i. Chords MN and RS intersect internally at point D. [Given]

 ∴ MD × DN = RD × DS [Theorem of internal division of chords]

 ∴ 8 × DN = 15 × 4

 ∴ DN = 15×4 8

 ∴ DN = 7.5 units

 ii. Let the value of RD be x.

 RS = RD + DS [R – D – S]

 ∴ 18 = x + DS

 ∴ DS = 18 – x

 Now, MD × DN = RD × DS [Theorem of internal division of chords]

 ∴ 9 × 8 = x(18 – x)

 ∴ 72 = 18x – x 2

 ∴ x2 – 18x + 72 = 0

 ∴ x2 – 12x – 6x + 72 = 0

 ∴ x (x – 12) – 6 (x – 12) = 0

 ∴ (x – 12) (x – 6) = 0

 ∴ x – 12 = 0 or x – 6 = 0

 ∴ x = 12 or x = 6

 ∴ DS = 18 – 12 or DS = 18 – 6

 ∴ DS = 6 units or DS = 12 units

Question 3.

 In the adjoining figure, O is the centre of the circle and B is a point of contact. Seg OE ⊥ seg AD, AB = 12, AC = 8, find

 i. AD

 ii. DC

 iii. DE.

![Image 5: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.5 3](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.5-3.png?resize=165%2C139&ssl=1)

 Solution:

 i. Line AB is the tangent at point B and seg AD is the secant. [Given]

 ∴ AC × AD = AB 2 [Tangent secant segments theorem]

 ∴ 8 × AD = 122

 ∴ 8 × AD = 144

 ∴ AD = 144 8

 ∴ AD = 18 units

 ii. AD = AC + DC [A – C – D]

 ∴ 18 = 8 + DC

 ∴ DC = 18 – 8

 ∴ DC = 10 units

 iii. seg OE ⊥ seg AD [Given]

 i.e. seg OE ⊥ seg CD [A – C – D]

 ∴ DE = 1 2 DC [Perpendicular drawn from the centre of the circle to the chord bisects the chord]

 = 1 2 × 10

 ∴ DE = 5 units

Question 4.

 In the adjoining figure, if PQ = 6, QR = 10, PS = 8, find TS.

 Solution:

 PR = PQ + QR [P-Q-R]

 ∴ PR = 6 + 10 = 16 units

![Image 6: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.5 4](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.5-4.png?resize=228%2C129&ssl=1)

 Chords TS and RQ intersect externally at point P.

 PQ × PR = PS × PT [Theorem of external division of chords]

 ∴ 6 × 16 = 8 × PT

 ∴ PT = 6×16 8 = 12 units

 But, PT = PS + TS [P – S – T]

 ∴ 12 = 8 + TS

 ∴ TS = 12 – 8

 ∴ TS = 4 units

Question 5.

 In the adjoining figure, seg EF is a diameter and seg DF is a tangent segment. The radius of the circle is r. Prove that, DE × GE = 4r 2.

 Given: seg EF is the diameter.

 seg DF is a tangent to the circle,

 radius = r

 To prove: DE × GE = 4r 2

 Construction: Join seg GF.

 seg DF is a tangent to the circle at F. [Given]

 ∴ ∠EFD = 90° (ii) [Tangent theorem]

 In ∆DFE,

 ∠EFD = 90 ° [From (ii)]

 seg FG ⊥ side DE [From (i)]

 ∴ ∆EFD ~ ∆EGF [Similarity of right angled triangles]

Question 1.

 Theorem: If an angle has its vertex on the circle, its one side touches the circle and the other intersects the circle in one more point, then the measure of the angle is half the measure of its intercepted arc. (Textbook pg.no. 75 and 76)

![Image 9: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.5 7](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.5-7.png?resize=585%2C189&ssl=1)

 Given: ∠ABC is any angle, whose vertex B lies on the circle with centre M.

 Line BC is tangent at B and line BA is secant intersecting the circle at point A.

 Arc ADB is intercepted by ∠ABC.

 To prove: ∠ABC = 1 2 m(arc ADB)

 Proof:

 Case I: Centre M lies on arm BA of ∠ABC.

 ∠MBC = 90° [Trangnet theorem]

![Image 10: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.5 8](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.5-8.png?resize=157%2C168&ssl=1)

 i.e. ∠ABC 90° (i) [A – M – B]

 arc ADB is a semicircular arc.

 ∴ m(arc ADB) = 180° (ii) [Measure ofa semicircle is 180°]

 ∴ ∠ABC = 1 2 m(arc ADB) [(From (i) and (ii)]

Case II: Centre M lies in the exterior of ∠ABC.

 Draw radii MA and MB.

 ∴ ∠MBA = ∠MAB [Isosceles triangle theorem]

![Image 11: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.5 9](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.5-9.png?resize=154%2C155&ssl=1)

 Let, ∠MHA = ∠MAB =x, ∠ABC = y In ∆ABM,

 ∠AMB + ∠MBA + ∠MAB = 180° [Sum of the measures of all the angles of a triangle is 1800]

 ∴ ∠AMB + x + x = 180°

 ∴ ∠AMB = 180° – 2x …… (i)

 Now, ∠MBC = ∠MBA + ∠ABC [Angle addition property]

 ∴ 90° = x + y [Tangent theorem]

 ∴ x = 90° – y ……(ii)

 ∠AMB = 180° – 2 (90° – y) [From (i) and (ii)]

 ∴ ∠AMB = 180° – 180° + 2y

 ∴ 2y = ∠AMB

 ∴ y = 1 2 ∠AMB

 ∴ ∠ABC = 1 2 ∠AMB

 ∴ ∠ABC = 1 2 m(arc ADB) [Definition of measure of minor arc]

Case III: Centre M lies in the interior of ∠ABC.

 Ray BE is the opposite ray of ray BC.

 Now, ∠ABE = 1 2 m (arc AFB) (i) [Proved in case II]

![Image 12: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Practice Set 3.5 10](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.5-10.png?resize=173%2C155&ssl=1)

 ∠ABC + ∠ABE = 180° [Angles in a linear pair]

 ∴ 180 – ∠ABC = ∠ABE

 ∴ 180 – ∠ABC = 1 2 m(arc AFB) [From (i)]

 = 1 2 [360 – m (arc ADB)]

 ∴ 180 – ∠ABC = 180 – 1 2 m(arc ADB)

 ∴ -∠ABC = – 1 2 m(arc ADB)

 ∴ ∠ABC = 1 2 m(arc ADB)

Question 2.

 We have proved the above theorem by drawing seg AC and seg DB. Can the theorem be proved by drawing seg AD and seg CB, instead of seg AC and seg DB? (Textbook pg. no. 77)

 Solution:

 Yes, the theorem can be proved by drawing seg AD and seg CB.

 Given: P is the centre of circle, chords AB and CD intersect internally at point E.

 To prove: AE × EB = CE × ED

 Proof:

 In ∆CEB and ∆AED,

 ∠CEB = ∠DEA [Vertically opposite angles]

 ∠CBE = ∠ADE [Angles inscribed in the same arc]

 ∴ ∆CEB ~ ∆AED [by AA test of similarity]

 ∴ C E A E = E B E D [Corresponding sides of similar triangles]

 ∴ AE × EB = CE × ED

Question 3.

 In figure, seg PQ is a diameter of a circle with centre O. R is any point on the circle, seg RS ⊥ seg PQ. Prove that, SR is the geometric mean of PS and SQ. [That is, SR 2 = PS × SQ] (Textbook pg. no. 81)

 Proof:

 ∴ seg OS ⊥ chord RT [R – S – T, P – S – O]

 ∴ segSR = segTS (i) [Perpendicular drawn from the centre of the circle to the chord bisects the chord]

 Chords PQ and RT intersect internally at point S.

 ∴ SR × TS = PS × SQ [Theorem of internal division of chords]

 ∴ SR × SR = PS × SQ [From (i)]

Question 4.

 Theorem: If secants containing chords AB and CD of a circle intersect outside the circle in point E, then

 Proof:

Question 5.

 Theorem: Point E is in the exterior of a circle. A secant through E intersects the circle at points A and B, and a tangent through E touches the circle at point T, then EA × EB = ET 2.

Question  
In the adjoining figure, ray PQ touches the circle at point Q. PQ = 12, PR = 8. Find PS and RS.

Method  
Use the tangent–secant theorem: if a tangent from an external point P touches the circle at Q and a secant from P meets the circle at R and S (with R between P and S), then
(PQ)^2 = (external part of secant) × (entire secant) = PR × PS.
Diagram cue: P, R, S are collinear with R between P and S; PQ is tangent at Q.

Working  
Given PQ = 12 and PR = 8. Apply the theorem:
(PQ)^2 = PR × PS
=> 12^2 = 8 × PS
=> 144 = 8 × PS
=> PS = 144 ÷ 8 = 18 units.

Now PS = PR + RS, so
RS = PS − PR = 18 − 8 = 10 units.

Final answer  
PS = 18 units  
RS = 10 units

Question
In the adjoining figure, chords MN and RS intersect at point D.

i. If RD = 15, DS = 4, MD = 8 find DN  
ii. If RS = 18, MD = 9, DN = 8 find DS

Diagram cue: The chords intersect inside the circle at D. From the given segment labels we use the order R–D–S on chord RS and M–D–N on chord MN.

Method
When two chords of a circle cross at an interior point, the product of the lengths of the two segments of one chord equals the product of the lengths of the two segments of the other chord:
(MD)(DN) = (RD)(DS).
Use this relation to find the unknown segment in each part.

Working
i. Given RD = 15, DS = 4, MD = 8. Use (MD)(DN) = (RD)(DS).
8 × DN = 15 × 4
8 DN = 60
DN = 60 / 8
DN = 7.5 (units)

ii. Given RS = 18, MD = 9, DN = 8. Let RD = x, then DS = RS − RD = 18 − x.
Use (MD)(DN) = (RD)(DS):
9 × 8 = x(18 − x)
72 = 18x − x^2
Rearrange to a standard quadratic:
x^2 − 18x + 72 = 0
Factor:
(x − 6)(x − 12) = 0
So x = 6 or x = 12.

Find DS for each x:
If x = 6, DS = 18 − 6 = 12 (units).
If x = 12, DS = 18 − 12 = 6 (units).

Final answer
i. DN = 7.5 units.  
ii. DS = 12 units or DS = 6 units (both values are possible corresponding to RD = 6 or RD = 12).

### Diagram reference

Question
In the adjoining figure, O is the centre of the circle and B is the point of contact. OE ⟂ AD, AB = 12, AC = 8. Find
i. AD
ii. DC
iii. DE

Method
- Use the tangent–secant power theorem: (tangent length)^2 = (product of the secant's external part and whole secant).
- Use subtraction to get DC from AD and AC.
- Use the property: the perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects that chord; here OE ⟂ CD so E is the midpoint of CD.

Working
1. By the tangent–secant theorem at external point A:
   AB^2 = AC × AD.
   Substitute AB = 12 and AC = 8:
   12^2 = 8 × AD
   144 = 8 × AD
   AD = 144 / 8 = 18.

2. DC = AD − AC = 18 − 8 = 10.

3. OE is perpendicular to the chord CD, so it bisects CD. Hence
   DE = DC / 2 = 10 / 2 = 5.

Final answer
i. AD = 18 units
ii. DC = 10 units
iii. DE = 5 units

Question  
In the adjoining figure, PQ = 6, QR = 10, PS = 8. Chords TS and RQ intersect externally at point P. Find TS.

Method  
Use the external-secant theorem: for two secants from an external point P that meet the circle at Q,R and S,T respectively (with Q and S nearer to P), the products of the external segment and the whole secant are equal:
PQ · PR = PS · PT.
Also PR = PQ + QR and PT = PS + TS.

Working
1. Compute the whole secant PR:
PR = PQ + QR = 6 + 10 = 16 units.

2. Apply the external-secant relation:
PQ · PR = PS · PT
6 · 16 = 8 · PT
96 = 8 · PT
PT = 96 / 8 = 12 units.

3. Find TS from PT = PS + TS:
TS = PT − PS = 12 − 8 = 4 units.

Final answer  
TS = 4 units.

Question

In the figure, EF is a diameter of a circle of radius r, and DF is the tangent at F. Prove that DE × GE = 4r^2, where G is the second intersection of line DE with the circle (the first intersection is E).

Method

Put the circle in a convenient coordinate system, compute the coordinates of E, F, D and the second intersection G of the line DE with the circle, find the lengths DE and EG, and show their product equals 4r^2.

Working

1. Place the circle with centre O at the origin and radius r. Then choose the diameter EF along the x-axis:
   - E = (−r, 0)
   - F = ( r, 0 )

2. The tangent at F is the vertical line x = r. Let D be any point on this tangent, D = (r, d) for some real d.

3. Equation of the line through D and E:
   Slope m = (d − 0)/(r − (−r)) = d/(2r).
   Thus the line DE has equation y = (d/(2r))(x + r).

4. Find the other intersection G of this line with the circle x^2 + y^2 = r^2.
   Substitute y into the circle equation:
   x^2 + [d^2/(4r^2)](x + r)^2 = r^2.
   Multiply by 4r^2:
   (4r^2 + d^2) x^2 + 2d^2 r x + (d^2 r^2 − 4r^4) = 0.

   One root is x = −r (point E). Let the other root be xG. By using the factor (x + r) or Vieta's formula, compute xG:
   Sum of roots = −(2d^2 r)/(4r^2 + d^2), so
   xG = −(2d^2 r)/(4r^2 + d^2) − (−r)
       = r (4r^2 − d^2)/(4r^2 + d^2).

5. Compute xG + r (this is the x-displacement from E to G):
   xG + r = r(4r^2 − d^2)/(4r^2 + d^2) + r
          = 8 r^3/(4r^2 + d^2).

6. Since G lies on the circle, yG^2 = r^2 − xG^2. Compute yG^2 explicitly:
   xG^2 = r^2(4r^2 − d^2)^2/(4r^2 + d^2)^2,
   so
   yG^2 = r^2 − xG^2
        = r^2[ (4r^2 + d^2)^2 − (4r^2 − d^2)^2 ]/(4r^2 + d^2)^2
        = r^2[16 r^2 d^2]/(4r^2 + d^2)^2
        = 16 r^4 d^2/(4r^2 + d^2)^2.

7. Compute EG^2 = (xG + r)^2 + yG^2:
   (xG + r)^2 = (8 r^3)^2/(4r^2 + d^2)^2 = 64 r^6/(4r^2 + d^2)^2,
   so
   EG^2 = [64 r^6 + 16 r^4 d^2]/(4r^2 + d^2)^2
         = 16 r^4 (4r^2 + d^2)/(4r^2 + d^2)^2
         = 16 r^4/(4r^2 + d^2).

   Hence EG = 4 r^2 / sqrt(4r^2 + d^2).

8. Compute DE: distance between D(r,d) and E(−r,0):
   DE = sqrt((r − (−r))^2 + (d − 0)^2)
      = sqrt(4r^2 + d^2).

9. Multiply DE and EG:
   DE × EG = sqrt(4r^2 + d^2) × (4 r^2 / sqrt(4r^2 + d^2)) = 4 r^2.

Final answer

DE × GE = 4 r^2, as required.

Question 1.

Given
- ∠ABC has its vertex B on a circle with centre M.
- Ray BC is tangent to the circle at B.
- Ray BA meets the circle again at A (so BA is a chord/ray through B meeting the circle at A).
- The arc intercepted by ∠ABC is arc ADB.

To prove
∠ABC = (1/2) m(arc ADB).

Proof/Steps

We consider three possible positions of the centre M relative to the angle ∠ABC.

Case I — Centre M lies on ray BA (i.e. A, M, B are collinear)
1. If M lies on BA, then AB is a diameter of the circle (since M is the centre and lies on the line through A and B).
2. The radius MB is perpendicular to the tangent BC at the point of contact B, so ∠MBC = 90°.
3. Because A–M–B are collinear, MB and BA are the same line, so ∠ABC = 90°.
4. The arc ADB is the semicircle opposite the diameter AB, so m(arc ADB) = 180°.
5. Thus ∠ABC = 90° = (1/2)·180° = (1/2) m(arc ADB).

Case II — Centre M lies outside the interior of ∠ABC
1. Join MA and MB. Triangle AMB is isosceles with MA = MB, so base angles are equal:
   ∠MAB = ∠MBA = x (say).
2. Let ∠ABC = y. In triangle AMB the angle sum gives
   ∠AMB + ∠MBA + ∠MAB = 180° ⇒ ∠AMB + x + x = 180° ⇒ ∠AMB = 180° − 2x.  (1)
3. The radius MB is perpendicular to tangent BC, so ∠MBC = 90°. But ∠MBC is the sum of ∠MBA and ∠ABC:
   ∠MBC = ∠MBA + ∠ABC ⇒ 90° = x + y ⇒ x = 90° − y.  (2)
4. Substitute (2) into (1):
   ∠AMB = 180° − 2(90° − y) = 180° − 180° + 2y = 2y.
   Hence y = (1/2) ∠AMB.
5. The central angle ∠AMB subtends arc ADB, so m(arc ADB) = ∠AMB. Therefore
   ∠ABC = y = (1/2) ∠AMB = (1/2) m(arc ADB).

Case III — Centre M lies inside ∠ABC
1. Let BE be the ray opposite BC (so B–C and B–E are opposite directions). Then ∠ABE is a linear pair with ∠ABC, so
   ∠ABE + ∠ABC = 180° ⇒ ∠ABE = 180° − ∠ABC.
2. Note that for angle ∠ABE the centre M lies outside that angle (because M is inside ∠ABC), so Case II applies to ∠ABE. Thus
   ∠ABE = (1/2) m(arc AFB),
   where arc AFB is the arc intercepted by ∠ABE.
3. Arc AFB and arc ADB are the two complementary arcs of the circle determined by A and B, so
   m(arc AFB) = 360° − m(arc ADB).
4. From step 1 and 2:
   180° − ∠ABC = (1/2) m(arc AFB) = (1/2) [360° − m(arc ADB)] = 180° − (1/2) m(arc ADB).
5. Subtract 180° from both sides and multiply by −1 to obtain
   ∠ABC = (1/2) m(arc ADB).

Result
In every possible position of the centre M relative to ∠ABC we obtain
∠ABC = (1/2) m(arc ADB).
Hence the measure of the angle formed at a point of the circle by a tangent and a chord (or secant) through that point equals half the measure of its intercepted arc.

Question 2

Given:
- P is the centre of a circle.
- AB and CD are two chords of the circle which meet at an interior point E.

To prove:
AE × EB = CE × ED

Construction:
Join A to D and C to B (draw segments AD and CB).

Diagram cue:
The textbook diagram shows A, B, C, D on the circle and chords AB, CD intersecting at E inside the circle. No numerical lengths are given; the argument below uses only the cyclic nature of A, B, C, D and the intersection point E.

Proof / Steps:
1. Consider triangles ΔCEB and ΔAED.

2. The angles at E in these two triangles are vertically opposite:
   ∠CEB = ∠DEA.

3. Next we compare the other pair of angles:
   - Point B lies on the circle, and the angle ∠CBE is formed by the chord BC and the line BE.
   - Point D lies on the circle, and the angle ∠ADE is formed by the chord AD and the line DE.
   Because A, B, C, D are concyclic, these two angles subtend the same arc of the circle (they stand on the same chord-pair of the circle), therefore
   ∠CBE = ∠ADE.

   (Thus the two triangles have a second pair of equal angles.)

4. From steps 2 and 3, by the AA criterion, ΔCEB ~ ΔAED.

5. From similarity, corresponding sides are proportional. In particular,
   CE / AE = BE / DE.

6. Cross-multiplying this proportion gives
   AE × EB = CE × ED.

Result (Final answer):
AE × EB = CE × ED. Hence the theorem is proved by drawing AD and CB.

### Diagram reference

![Worked diagram 1](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.5-11.png?resize=150%2C132&ssl=1)

Question
In the figure, PQ is a diameter of a circle with centre O. R is any point on the circle, and RS ⟂ PQ. Prove that SR is the geometric mean of PS and SQ; that is, SR^2 = PS × SQ.

Method
Extend the line RS to meet the circle again at T (so R, S, T are collinear). Use (1) the fact that a radius perpendicular to a chord bisects the chord, and (2) the intersecting-chords theorem (product of segments of one chord equals product of segments of the other chord when two chords intersect inside a circle).

Working
1. Construction: Produce ray RS beyond S to meet the circle again at T. Then R, S, T are collinear and RT is the chord through R and T.

2. Since PQ is a diameter, O lies on line PQ. Given RS ⟂ PQ, the line OS (a part of PQ) is perpendicular to RS. Because R, S, T are collinear, OS is also perpendicular to chord RT. 

3. A radius (OS) perpendicular to a chord (RT) bisects that chord. Therefore S is the midpoint of RT, so SR = ST.   (1)

4. Chords PQ and RT intersect at S. By the intersecting-chords theorem,
   PS × SQ = SR × ST.   (2)

5. Substitute ST = SR from (1) into (2):
   PS × SQ = SR × SR = SR^2.

Final answer
SR^2 = PS × SQ, as required.

### Diagram reference

![Worked diagram 1](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.5-12.png?resize=166%2C163&ssl=1)

Question 4

Given:
- A circle with two secants through an external point E meeting the circle at A, B (on one secant) and C, D (on the other secant).
- Chords AB and CD are therefore cut off by the secants through E.

To prove:
AE × EB = CE × ED

Construction:
Join A to D and B to C.

Diagram cue:
The diagram shows two straight lines through E that cut the circle at A, B and at C, D respectively (with A and B on one secant and C and D on the other). No additional numerical values are assumed.

Proof / Steps:
1. Consider triangles ΔADE and ΔCEB.

2. ∠AED and ∠CEB are equal because they are vertically opposite angles formed by the two intersecting secant lines at E.

3. ∠ADE and ∠CBE are equal because they stand on the same segment of the circle (each subtends the same arc). Hence the second pair of angles of the two triangles are equal.

4. From steps 2 and 3, ΔADE and ΔCEB have two equal angles; therefore the triangles are similar (AA criterion).

5. From the similarity of ΔADE and ΔCEB, corresponding sides are proportional:
AE : CE = ED : EB.

6. Cross-multiplying this proportion gives
AE × EB = CE × ED.

Result:
AE × EB = CE × ED.

### Diagram reference

![Worked diagram 1](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.5-13.png?resize=237%2C132&ssl=1)
solutionPages.page-10:
Question 5

Given
- Point E lies outside a circle.
- A secant through E meets the circle at A and B (points A and B lie on the same line with E).
- A tangent from E touches the circle at T.

To prove
- EA × EB = ET^2

Construction
- Join T to A and T to B (draw segments TA and TB).

Proof / Steps
1. Note that A, E, B are collinear (E lies on the secant through A and B). Therefore rays EA and EB are opposite directions. Hence the angle between EA and ET equals the angle between ET and EB. In symbol form:
   ∠AET = ∠TEB. (These are the two angles made at E by the same straight line and the ray ET.)

2. By the tangent–chord property: the angle made by a tangent and a chord through the point of contact is equal to the angle in the alternate segment of the circle. Applying this to tangent ET and chord TA gives
   ∠ETA = ∠EBT.

3. From steps 1 and 2, triangles EAT and ETB have two pairs of equal angles:
   ∠AET = ∠TEB and ∠ETA = ∠EBT.
   Therefore triangles EAT and ETB are similar (AA similarity).

4. From similarity of triangles EAT and ETB, corresponding sides are proportional. Taking the sides around E and T gives:
   EA / ET = ET / EB.

5. Cross-multiplying the proportion yields:
   EA × EB = ET^2.

Result
EA × EB = ET^2, as required.

### Diagram reference

![Worked diagram 1](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.5-14.png?resize=185%2C157&ssl=1)

Question
In the figure in the above example, if segments PR and RQ are drawn, what is the nature of triangle PRQ?

Method
Use the property of an inscribed angle subtending a diameter (Thales' theorem): an angle formed at a point on a circle by joining the endpoints of a diameter is a right angle.

Diagram cue
The figure shows P and Q as endpoints of a diameter of the circle and R as another point on the circle. No other numerical lengths are assumed.

Working
1. Since PQ is a diameter, the central angle POQ (with O the centre) subtending arc PQ is 180° (a straight line).
2. The inscribed angle PRQ subtends the same arc PQ. By the inscribed-angle property, an inscribed angle equals half the measure of the central angle that subtends the same arc.
3. Therefore ∠PRQ = 1/2 × ∠POQ = 1/2 × 180° = 90°.

Final answer
Triangle PRQ is a right-angled triangle; the right angle is at R (∠PRQ = 90°).

### Diagram reference

![Worked diagram 1](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Practice-Set-3.5-15.png?resize=142%2C140&ssl=1)

Question
Have you previously proved the property proved in the above example?

Method
Use similarity of right triangles (AA criterion) to obtain a proportion between corresponding sides, then rearrange to get the required relation. (Diagram cue: the textbook diagram shows two right triangles ΔPSR and ΔRSQ with right angles at R and with S as a common vertex.)

Working
1. From the diagram cue, ∠PRS = ∠SRQ = 90°. Both triangles ΔPSR and ΔRSQ are right-angled at R.  
2. They also have the common angle at S: ∠PSR = ∠RSQ.  
   Therefore, by AA (two equal angles), ΔPSR ~ ΔRSQ.

3. From similarity, corresponding sides are proportional. Choose the correspondence that gives the middle side SR between the two triangles:
   PS : SR = SR : SQ.

4. Cross-multiply the proportion:
   SR × SR = PS × SQ
   i.e., SR^2 = PS × SQ.

Final answer
Yes. This is the geometric mean property: for the similar right triangles ΔPSR and ΔRSQ we get PS : SR = SR : SQ, hence SR^2 = PS × SQ. In words, SR is the geometric mean of PS and SQ.

notes.content:
Balbharti [Maharashtra State Board Class 10 Maths Solutions](https://maharashtraboardsolutions.com/maharashtra-state-board-class-10-maths-solutions/) covers the Problem Set 3 Geometry 10th Class Maths Part 2 Answers Solutions Chapter 3 Circle.

### Class 10 Maths Part 2 Problem Set 3 Chapter 3 Circle Questions With Answers Maharashtra Board

Problem Set 3 Geometry Class 10 Question 1.

 Four alternative answers for each of the following questions are given. Choose the correct alternative.

i. Two circles of radii 5.5 cm and 3.3 cm respectively touch each other. What is the distance between their centres?

 (A) 4.4 cm

 (B) 8.8 cm

 (C) 2.2 cm

 (D) 8.8 or 2.2 cm

 Answer: (D)

 Two circles can touch each other internally or externally.

 ∴ Distance between centres = 5.5 + 3.3 or 5.5 – 3.3 = 8.8 or 2.2

ii. Two circles intersect each other such that each circle passes through the centre of the other. If the distance between their centres is 12, what is the radius of each circle?

 (A) 6 cm

 (B) 12 cm

 (C) 24 cm

 (D) can’t say

 Answer: (B)

 PQ is the radius = 12 cm

![Image 3: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Problem Set 3 1](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/01/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Problem-Set-3-1.png?resize=185%2C117&ssl=1)

iii. A circle touches all sides of a parallelogram. So the parallelogram must be a __________.

 (A) rectangle

 (B) rhombus

 (C) square

 (D) trapezium

 Answer: (B)

 ꠸ABCD is a rhombus.

 Note: It cannot be square as the angles are not mentioned as 90°.

![Image 4: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Problem Set 3 2](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/01/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Problem-Set-3-2.png?resize=191%2C135&ssl=1)

iv. Length of a tangent segment drawn from a point which is at a distance 12.5 cm from the centre of a circle is 12 cm, find the diameter of the circle.

 (A) 25 cm

 (B) 24 cm

 (C) 7 cm

 (D) 14 cm

 Answer: (C)

![Image 5: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Problem Set 3 3](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/01/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Problem-Set-3-3.png?resize=201%2C142&ssl=1)

 In ∆OAB, ∠B = 90° [Tangent theorem]

 ∴ OA 2 = OB 2 + AB 2 [Pythagoras theorem]

 ∴ 12.5 2 = OB 2 + 12 2

 ∴ OB 2 = 156.25- 144

 ∴ OB = 12.25−−−−√ = 3.5 cm

 ∴ Diameter = 2 × OB = 2 × 3.5 = 7 cm

v. If two circles are touching externally, how many common tangents of them can be drawn?

 (A) One

 (B) Two

 (C) Three

 (D) Four

 Answer: (C)

 line l, line m and line n are the tangents.

![Image 6: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Problem Set 3 4](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/01/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Problem-Set-3-4.png?resize=243%2C163&ssl=1)

vi. ∠ACB is inscribed in arc ACB of a circle with centre O. If ∠ACB = 65°, find m(arc ACB).

 (A) 65°

 (B) 130°

 (C) 295°

 (D) 230°

 Answer: (D)

 m∠ACB = 1 2 m(arc AB) [Inscribed angle theorem]

![Image 7: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Problem Set 3 5](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/01/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Problem-Set-3-5.png?resize=125%2C125&ssl=1)

 ∴ m(arc AB) = 2 m∠ACB =

 = 2 × 65

 = 130°

 m(arc ACB) = 360° – m(arc AB) [Measure of a circle is 360°]

 = 360° – 130°

 = 230°

vii. Chords AB and CD of a circle intersect inside the circle at point E. If AE = 5.6, EB = 10, CE = 8, find ED.

 (A) 7

 (B) 8

 (C) 11.2

 (D) 9

 Answer: (A)

 Chords AB and CD intersect

 internally at E.

 AE × EB = CE × ED [Theorem of internal division of chords]

![Image 8: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Problem Set 3 6](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/01/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Problem-Set-3-6.png?resize=149%2C130&ssl=1)

 ∴ 5.6 × 10 = 8 × ED

 ∴ ED = 7 units

viii. In a cyclic ꠸ABCD, twice the measure of ∠A is thrice the measure of ∠C. Find the measure of ∠C?

 (A) 36°

 (B) 72°

 (C) 90°

 (D) 108°

 Answer: (B)

 ∠A + ∠C = 180° [Theorem of cyclic quadrilateral]

 ∴ 2∠A + 2∠C = 2 × 180° [Multiplying both sides by 2]

 ∴ 3∠C + 2∠C = 360° [∵ 2∠A = 3∠C]

 ∴ 5∠C = 360°

 ∴ ∠C = 72°

ix. Points A, B, C are on a circle, such that m(arc AB) = m(arc BC) = 120°. No point, except point B, is common to the arcs. Which is the type of ∆ABC?

 (A) Equilateral triangle

 (B) Scalene triangle

 (C) Right angled triangle

 (D) Isosceles triangle

 Answer: (A)

 m(arc AB) + m(arc BC) + m(arc AC) = 360° [Measure of a circle is 360°]

 ∴ 120° + 120° + m (arc AC) = 360°

![Image 9: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Problem Set 3 7](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/01/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Problem-Set-3-7.png?resize=119%2C130&ssl=1)

 ∴ m(arc AC) = 120°

 ∴ arc AB = arc BC = arc AC

 ∴ seg AB ≅ seg BC ≅ seg AC [Corresponding chords of congruents arcs of a circle are congruent]

 ∴ ∆ABC is an equilateral triangle.

x. Seg XZ is a diameter of a circle. Point Y lies in its interior. How many of the following statements are true?

 (i) It is not possible that ∠XYZ is an acute angle.

 (ii) ∠XYZ can’t be a right angle.

 (iii) ∠XYZ is an obtuse angle.

 (iv) Can’t make a definite statement for measure of ∠XYZ.

 (A) Only one

 (B) Only two

 (C) Only three

 (D) All

 Answer: (C)

 x. seg XZ is the diameter.

 ∴ ∠XWZ is a right angle. [Angle inscribed in a semicircle]

![Image 10: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Problem Set 3 8](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/01/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Problem-Set-3-8.png?resize=154%2C136&ssl=1)

 Since, Y lies in the interior of ∆XWZ,

 ∴ ∠XYZ > 90°

 i.e., ∠XYZ is an obtuse angle.

Problem Set 3 Question 2.

 Line l touches a circle with centre O at point P. If radius of the circle is 9 cm, answer the following.

 i. What is d(O, P) = ? Why?

 ii. If d(O, Q) = 8 cm, where does the point Q lie?

 iii. If d(O, R) = 15 cm, how many locations of point R are on line l ?

 At what distance will each of them be from point P?

![Image 11: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Problem Set 3 9](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/01/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Problem-Set-3-9.png?resize=212%2C138&ssl=1)

 Solution:

 i. seg OP is the radius of the circle.

 ∴ d(0, P) = 9 cm

 ii. Here, 8 cm < 9 cm

 ∴ d(0, Q) < d(0, P)

 ∴ d(0, Q) < radius

 Point Q lies in the interior of the circle.

 iii. There can be two locations of point R on line l.

![Image 12: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Problem Set 3 10](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/01/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Problem-Set-3-10.png?resize=216%2C144&ssl=1)

 d(0, R) = 15 cm

 Now, in ∆OPR, ∠OPR = 90° [Tangent theorem]

 ∴ OR 2 = OP 2 + PR 2 [Pythagoras theorem]

 ∴ 15 2 = 9 2 + PR 2

 ∴ 225 = 81 + PR 2

 ∴ PR 2 = 225 – 81 = 144 [Taking square root of both sides]

 ∴ PR = 144−−−√

 = 12 cm

Standard 10th Geometry Problem Set 3 Question 3.

 In the adjoining figure, M is the centre of the circle and seg KL is a tangent segment. If MK = 12, KL = 6 3–√ ,then find

 i. Radius of the circle.

 ii. Measures of ∠K and ∠M.

![Image 13: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Problem Set 3 11](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/01/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Problem-Set-3-11.png?resize=198%2C135&ssl=1)

 Solution:

 i. Line KL is the tangent to the circle at point L and seg ML is the radius. [Given]

 ∴ ∠MLK = 90°…………. (i) [Tangent theorem]

 In ∆MLK, ∠MLK = 90°

 ∴ MK 2 = ML 2 + KL 2 [Pythagoras theorem]

 ∴ 12 2 = ML 2 + (6 3–√)2

 ∴ 144 = ML 2 + 108

 ∴ ML 2 = 144 – 108

 ∴ ML 2 = 36

 ∴ ML = 36−−√ = 6 units. [Taking square root of both sides]

 ∴ Radius of the circle is 6 units.

ii. We know that,

 ML = 1 2 MK

 ∴ ∠K = 30° …………… (ii) [Converse of 30° – 60° – 90° theorem]

 In ∆MLK ,

 ∠L = 90° [From (i)]

 ∠K = 30° [From (ii)]

 ∴ ∠M = 60° [Remaining angle of ∆MLK]

10th Class Geometry Problem Set 3 Question 4.

 In the adjoining figure, O is the centre of the circle. Seg AB, seg AC are tangent segments. Radius of the circle is r and l(AB) = r. Prove that, □ABOC is a square.

![Image 14: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Problem Set 3 12](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/01/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Problem-Set-3-12.png?resize=180%2C172&ssl=1)

 Given: O is the centre of circle.

 seg AB and seg AC are the tangents, radius = r, /(AB) = r.

 To prove: □ABOC is a square.

 Construction: Draw seg OB and seg OC.

 Proof:

 seg AB and seg AC are the tangents to the circle. [Given]

 ∴ AB = AC [Tangent segment theorem]

 But, AB = r [Given]

 ∴ AB = AC = r ……….. (i)

 Also, OB = OC = r ……….. (ii) [Radii of the same circle]

![Image 15: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Problem Set 3 13](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/01/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Problem-Set-3-13.png?resize=179%2C171&ssl=1)

 ∴ AB = AC = OB = OC [From (i) and (ii)]

 ∴ □ABOC is a rhombus.

 ∠OBA = 90° [Tangent theorem]

 ∴ □ABOC is a square [A rhombus is a square, if one of its angles is a right angle]

Question 5.

 In the adjoining figure, ꠸ABCD is a parallelogram. It circumscribes the circle with centre T. Points E, F, G, H are touching points. If AE = 4.5, EB = 5.5, find AD.

![Image 16: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Problem Set 3 14](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/01/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Problem-Set-3-14.png?resize=173%2C144&ssl=1)

 Solution:

 Let the values of DH and CF be x and y respectively.

 [ AE = AH = 4.5

 BE = BF = 5.5

 DH = DG = x

 CF = CG = y ] [Tangent segment theorem]

 □ABCD is a parallelogram. [Given]

![Image 17: Maharashtra Board Class 10 Maths Solutions Chapter 3 Circle Problem Set 3 15](https://i0.wp.com/www.learncram.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/01/Maharashtra-Board-Class-10-Maths-Solutions-Chapter-3-Circle-Problem-Set-3-15.png?resize=180%2C151&ssl=1)

 ∴ AB = CD [Opposite sides of a parallelogram]

 ∴ AE + BE = DG + CG [A – E – B, D – G – C]

 ∴ 4.5 + 5.5 = x + y

 ∴ x + y = 10 ……….. (i)

 Also, AD = BC [Opposite sides of a parallelogram]

 ∴ AH + DH = BF + CF [A – H – D, B – F – C]

 ∴ 4.5 + x = 5.5 + y

 ∴ x – y = 1 ………… (ii)

 Adding equations (i) and (ii), we get

 2x = 11

 ∴ x = 11 2 = 5.5

 ∴ AD = AH + DH [A – H – D]

 = 4.5 + 5.5

# Question 1

For each part, choose the correct alternative and show reasoning.

i. Two circles of radii 5.5 cm and 3.3 cm respectively touch each other. What is the distance between their centres?

Method  
When two circles touch, the distance between centres equals either the sum of radii (external contact) or the difference of radii (internal contact).

Working  
Sum = 5.5 + 3.3 = 8.8 cm  
Difference = 5.5 − 3.3 = 2.2 cm

Final answer  
(D) 8.8 or 2.2 cm

---

ii. Two circles intersect each other such that each circle passes through the centre of the other. If the distance between their centres is 12, what is the radius of each circle?

Method  
If each circle passes through the centre of the other, then the distance between centres equals the radius of each circle.

Working  
Distance between centres = 12 ⇒ radius = 12

Final answer  
(B) 12 cm

---

iii. A circle touches all sides of a parallelogram. So the parallelogram must be a __________.

Method  
A quadrilateral has an incircle (a circle tangent to all four sides) exactly when the sums of lengths of opposite sides are equal. In a parallelogram opposite sides are already equal; for the sums to match in the required way the adjacent sides must be equal, so all four sides are equal.

Working  
Let parallelogram ABCD have an incircle. Tangent segments from a vertex to the two adjacent tangency points are equal, so comparing around the parallelogram leads to AB = BC = CD = DA. Hence all sides equal.

Final answer  
(B) rhombus

---

iv. Length of a tangent segment drawn from a point which is at a distance 12.5 cm from the centre of a circle is 12 cm. Find the diameter of the circle.

Method  
The radius, the tangent segment and the line from centre to the external point form a right triangle: (distance from centre to point)^2 = radius^2 + (tangent length)^2. Solve for radius, then double it to get diameter.

Working  
Let centre O, external point P, tangent point T. OP = 12.5, PT = 12, OT = r.  
OP^2 = OT^2 + PT^2  
(12.5)^2 = r^2 + (12)^2  
156.25 = r^2 + 144  
r^2 = 156.25 − 144 = 12.25  
r = √12.25 = 3.5 cm  
Diameter = 2r = 7.0 cm

Final answer  
(C) 7 cm

---

v. If two circles are touching externally, how many common tangents of them can be drawn?

Method  
Compare positions:
- If two circles are separate and do not touch: 4 common tangents (two direct, two transverse).
- If they touch externally: the two transverse tangents coincide at the touching configuration into a single common tangent at the point of contact, while two direct tangents remain distinct. Thus total = 3.

Working  
External contact ⇒ 2 external (direct) tangents + 1 tangent at contact = 3

Final answer  
(C) Three

Question vi.
∠ACB is an inscribed angle of a circle with centre O. If ∠ACB = 65°, find the measure of arc ACB.

Method
An inscribed angle measures half the measure of its intercepted arc. The angle at C intercepts arc AB (the smaller arc between A and B). The arc ACB is the remaining (major) arc from A through C to B, so its measure equals 360° minus the measure of arc AB.

Diagram cue: The diagram shows an inscribed angle at C intercepting arc AB. No other numerical information in the diagram is needed.

Working
m(arc AB) = 2 × m(∠ACB) = 2 × 65° = 130°.
m(arc ACB) = 360° − m(arc AB) = 360° − 130° = 230°.

Final answer
230°.

---

Question vii.
Chords AB and CD of a circle intersect inside the circle at point E. If AE = 5.6, EB = 10, CE = 8, find ED.

Method
When two chords intersect inside a circle, the product of the segments of one chord equals the product of the segments of the other: AE × EB = CE × ED.

Diagram cue: The diagram shows chords AB and CD crossing at E; no other lengths are on the diagram.

Working
AE × EB = CE × ED
5.6 × 10 = 8 × ED
56 = 8 × ED
ED = 56 ÷ 8 = 7 units.

Final answer
7 units.

---

Question viii.
In a cyclic quadrilateral ABCD, twice the measure of ∠A equals three times the measure of ∠C. Find ∠C.

Method
Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary: ∠A + ∠C = 180°. Use the given relation 2∠A = 3∠C to express A in terms of C and solve.

Working
From 2∠A = 3∠C ⇒ ∠A = (3/2)∠C.
Substitute into ∠A + ∠C = 180°:
(3/2)∠C + ∠C = 180°
(5/2)∠C = 180°
∠C = 180° × (2/5) = 360°/5 = 72°.

Final answer
72°.

---

Question ix.
Points A, B, C lie on a circle with m(arc AB) = m(arc BC) = 120°. No point other than B is common to these arcs. What type of triangle is ΔABC?

Method
Equal arcs subtend equal chords. If the three arcs around the circle are equal, all three chords AB, BC, CA are equal, so the triangle with those sides is equilateral. Compute the third arc to confirm equality.

Working
Total circle measure = 360°. Given arc AB = 120° and arc BC = 120°, the remaining arc CA = 360° − 120° − 120° = 120°. Thus all three arcs are equal ⇒ all three chords AB, BC, CA are equal ⇒ ΔABC has three equal sides.

Final answer
Equilateral triangle.

Question 1
Given: In a circle, m(arc AB) = 120° and m(arc BC) = 120°. Find m(arc AC) and classify triangle ABC.

Method
Use the fact that the measures of the three arcs that together make the whole circle sum to 360°. Equal arcs subtend equal chords, and equal chords subtend equal sides in the corresponding triangle.

Working
- Sum of the three arcs AB, BC and AC equals 360°:
  m(arc AB) + m(arc BC) + m(arc AC) = 360°.
- Substitute the given values:
  120° + 120° + m(arc AC) = 360°.
- Solve for m(arc AC):
  m(arc AC) = 360° − 240° = 120°.
- So m(arc AB) = m(arc BC) = m(arc AC) = 120°. 
- Equal arcs imply equal corresponding chords: AB = BC = AC.
- A triangle with all three sides equal is an equilateral triangle; each interior angle = 60°.

Final answer
m(arc AC) = 120°. Triangle ABC is an equilateral triangle (all sides congruent, all angles 60°).

---

Question 2
Given: Segment XZ is a diameter of a circle. Point Y lies in the interior of the circle. Which of the following statements are true?
(i) It is not possible that ∠XYZ is an acute angle.
(ii) ∠XYZ can’t be a right angle.
(iii) ∠XYZ is an obtuse angle.
(iv) Can’t make a definite statement for measure of ∠XYZ.
Options: (A) Only one, (B) Only two, (C) Only three, (D) All.

Method
Recall: any inscribed angle that subtends a diameter is a right angle (90°) when its vertex lies on the circle. Compare the angle subtended by the same chord XZ for a point Y inside the circle with the inscribed angle for a point W on the circle: as the vertex moves from the circle into the interior on the same side of XZ, the subtended angle increases. Use this to determine whether ∠XYZ can be acute, right or obtuse.

Diagram cue: If needed, choose a point W on the circle such that ∠XWZ = 90° (angle in a semicircle). The reasoning below uses that construction; no additional numerical labels are assumed.

Working
- For any point W on the circle (on the semicircle determined by diameter XZ), the inscribed angle ∠XWZ = 90° because XZ is a diameter.
- If Y is a point inside the circle on the same side of the line XZ as W and lies inside triangle XWZ, then the rays YX and YZ lie inside the angle ∠XWZ, so ∠XYZ > ∠XWZ = 90°. Thus ∠XYZ is greater than 90° (i.e., obtuse).
- If Y is any interior point of the circle (not on the circumferential circle), the measure of ∠XYZ cannot be 90° (a right angle occurs only when the vertex is on the circle) and cannot be acute (an acute angle would be less than 90°, but interior points produce angles ≥90°). In the special collinear case when Y lies on segment XZ, ∠XYZ = 180° (a straight angle); otherwise interior positions give angles strictly between 90° and 180°.
- Therefore:
  (i) True — ∠XYZ cannot be acute.
  (ii) True — ∠XYZ cannot be right (that requires Y on the circle).
  (iii) True in the noncollinear interior case — ∠XYZ is obtuse (strictly >90°) for interior points not on XZ; if Y lies on XZ the angle is 180° (still not acute or right).
  (iv) False — we can make a definite statement: the angle is ≥ 90° and, except for the straight-angle collinear case, strictly > 90°.

Final answer
Three of the statements (i), (ii) and (iii) are true. Correct option: (C) Only three.

Question
Line l touches a circle with centre O at point P. The radius of the circle is 9 cm. Answer:

i. What is d(O, P)? Why?  
ii. If d(O, Q) = 8 cm, where does the point Q lie?  
iii. If d(O, R) = 15 cm, how many locations of point R are on line l? At what distance will each of them be from point P?

Method
- Use the definition of radius and the property that the radius to the point of contact is perpendicular to the tangent line.
- Compare distances from O with the radius to decide whether a point is inside, on, or outside the circle.
- For points on the tangent line at a given distance from O, form the right triangle O–P–R (P is foot of perpendicular) and apply Pythagoras to find PR.

Working
i. P is the point of contact of the tangent with the circle, so OP is a radius. Given radius = 9 cm.  
Therefore d(O, P) = 9 cm.

ii. Given d(O, Q) = 8 cm. Since 8 cm < radius 9 cm, Q lies at a distance from O less than the radius.  
Hence Q is inside (in the interior of) the circle.

iii. Let R be a point on line l with d(O, R) = 15 cm. Because OP is perpendicular to l at P, for any point R on l the triangle OPR is right-angled at P. Use Pythagoras:
OR^2 = OP^2 + PR^2.
Substitute OR = 15 cm and OP = 9 cm:
15^2 = 9^2 + PR^2
225 = 81 + PR^2
PR^2 = 225 − 81 = 144
PR = √144 = 12 cm.

There are two possible points R on the line l at distance 15 cm from O: one on each side of P along the tangent. Each is 12 cm from P.

Final answer
i. d(O, P) = 9 cm, because P is a point on the circle and OP is the radius.  

ii. Q lies inside the circle (interior), since d(O, Q) = 8 cm < 9 cm.  

iii. There are two possible positions for R on line l (one on each side of P). Each such R is 12 cm away from P.
